Mr. Speaker, on Monday last, in reply to a question from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), the Prime Minister (Mr. St-Laurent) indicated that I would make a statement as to whether it was intended to proceed at this session with the amendments to the Municipal Grants Act. As I stated, I think last week, the government had hoped to be able to proceed with that measure this session, but the legislative program has been heavy, and in view of the fact that the amendments would not be operative until the calendar year 1955, the usual municipal year, no prejudice would be suffered by the measure standing over until the next session.
It would be the government's intention to introduce the measure at the earliest possible moment at that session. There is an item in my estimates of some $3 million for the grants for the calendar year, and when that item is called we shall have an opportunity to discuss the matter and I can indicate, in a general way, the nature of the amendments which the government has in mind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: DECLINE IN EXPORTS OF TOBACCO TO HOLLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) a question in connection with the decline of exports of Canadian tobacco to Holland. His question 83276-383J
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus may be found at page 5829 of Hansard for Friday, June 11. Inquiries have been made in this respect and I can now inform the house that the decline in Canadian exports of tobacco to The Netherlands can be attributed to the fact that our sales in that market in recent years have been made up of lower grades of tobacco. As a result of favourable growing and marketing conditions in Canada we have not had as much of these grades of tobacco for export during the last two or three years.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Prudham for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Harkness, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. McCullough (Moose Mountain).

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I had a speech prepared that could in no sense be described as a controversial speech, but in view of some of the statements made during the debate yesterday perhaps I will not be able to conclude my remarks without making some critical references to some of the statements made.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) spent some time dealing with what this proposal is likely to cost the treasury of Canada. He estimated, first of all, that it might cost the taxpayers $100 million, or perhaps $130 million, or, if the price really went down, it might cost $260 million.
The conclusion one would draw from his remarks would be that the Canadian farmer should be left holding the bag. We are in a critical position. Our whole argument is that all of Canada should stand behind the wheat producers at this critical time and I hope, before I conclude, that I will be able to demonstrate that this is not an unreasonable request.
Let me remind the hon. member for Eglinton that a year ago, on May 6 to be exact, he and members of his party who were here were prepared to support a price for wheat 25 cents higher than the price proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). Of course, it could happen that the election last year might have been a factor in this regard, but the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) and all the other Conservative members who were here were quite prepared to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus at that time. That amendment appears on page 4856 of Hansard for May 6, 1953, and reads as follows:
this house is of the opinion that consideration should be given to an increase of 25 cents in the initial payment for No. 1 Northern wheat basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver for the crop year beginning August 1, 1953, so that the said initial payment will be $1.65 per bushel.
If that was a good proposal a year ago I submit that the proposal which is before us now is also a good one. I -think it is not unreasonable to expect the government of Canada to take some responsibility for supporting the price of wheat.
I might mention to hon. members opposite that apparently only two of the Liberal members from Saskatchewan who voted against this proposal a year ago came back to parliament after the election. They were the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison), and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer). Apparently it was not too easy for other hon. members to justify their stand in the province of Saskatchewan.
I wish to make it very clear that the members of this group in supporting this subamendment are not criticizing in any way the wheat board or orderly marketing. We have made it quite clear that we would be most unhappy if the opposition should be called upon to look after the marketing of farm products.
I should mention that the share of national income that went to agriculture during the years when the Conservatives were last in power amounted to 7-6 per cent in 1930, 2-9 per cent in 1931, 4-1 per cent in 1932, 3 per cent in 1933, and 6 per cent in 1934. Now, I am not satisfied with the 8-8 per cent of the national income which went to agriculture in 1953, but I must admit very frankly that having 8-8 per cent of the national income is a great deal better than having 2-9 per cent, and the fact that the people of Saskatchewan have been unwilling to elect Conservative members to the legislature since 1929 would indicate that they are very unhappy when they think of the terrible years during the thirties. Therefore, I would like to make it very clear again that we support the wheat board and orderly marketing.
Now, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) should perhaps be reminded that this is not a motion of want of confidence in the government. If this motion should carry, the procedure would be exactly as it was in August, 1946, when we had a similar motion before the house and when the hon. member for Rosthern and I voted on the same side on this important issue. Let me remind the house of the nature of the amendment which

I had the honour to move on August 27, 1946. This appears on page 5425 of August 27, 1946, and reads as follows:
This house desires to record its opinion that consideration should be given to the continuance of the milk subsidy so as to ensure adequate return to milk producers and make possible the consumption of milk for the nutrition of the Canadian people without any further increase in the price thereof to the consumers.
When the vote was called the hon. member for Rosthern -and I were on the same side, and the vote was 69 for and 41 against, and the government at that time was not defeated. The present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) then moved that the house go into committee of supply and the business of the house was then continued.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if it was in order for the hon. member for Rosthern to vote for a principle he thought then was sound it would be quite in order for him to vote now in support of the subamendment which is before the house.
However, I take it that he is opposed to the content of the subamendment and he does not think the taxpayers of Canada should be called upon to place -any floor under the price of wheat. He thinks that the farmers should engage in a price war with our powerful neighbours to the south who have all the resources of their treasury to subsidize wheat for export.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member knows that he is not correctly representing what I said. I said I believed the Liberal party believes in the principle of floor prices and that they believe in giving a square deal to the farmer in order to see that he gets his fair share of the national income. That policy I support. But I do not support a motion which upholds the idea that the whole marketing system has failed.

Mr. Speaker, that statement sounds as though it confirms what I previously stated, namely that the hon. member for Rosthern is not prepared to support any legislation that will give the farmers an assurance that the price of wheat is not going to go down into the cellar again.

Mr. Speaker, I am supporting a government which has said that it will make an initial payment which will constitute a fair floor. That is exactly what I am supporting. The hon. member is misrepresenting the situation.

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus an unmixed blessing. They are concerned about the effect that this is going to have on world trade.
From the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has come their June dispatch which complains about the diminishing share of the 'national income going to the farmer, taking into consideration the farm cost of living. The real net farm income in 1953 was 10 per cent lower than in 1952 and 25 per cent lower than in the peak year of 1951. Using the five years 1925-29 as the base period, the parity ratio reached a peak of 111 for 1948, fell to 106 in 1949, rose to 110 in 1951 and fell for two years to the low level of 87-4. At the present time the cost of goods and services purchased by farmers averaged 3 per cent higher in 1951 whereas the wholesale price of farm products averaged 18 per cent lower. Just this morning 1 received a letter from the Manitoba farmers union, a letter addressed to all western members of the House of Commons, and it suggests with respect to the very bad news announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) last week that it is hard for western farmers to believe that the government expects them to compete with the United States treasury. They remind us of the statement made by the late prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, in his radio broadcast of December 4, 1943, when he said:
If to help win the war the farmers are asked to accept ceiling prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to assure them against agricultural depression after the war.
I must take some responsibility for the fact that those of us from western Canada have not done the best public relations job in presenting the problem to our people. I came here in 1940 from an area that had very rough times all during the thirties. I considered that it was one of my duties to try to see that the people whom I represented had their fair share of the national income. I probably could be open to the criticism that the conditions I described possibly did not represent the facts for everybody in the area, but that was the area to which those people came who had lost everything in the drought areas of the province in order that they could start over again on heavy bush land. I admit very frankly that during the last ten years the people of my constituency have handled a good deal more money than they did in the previous ten years, but we are not going to be satisfied until we have our Jiair share of the national income.
I think all farm organizations and farm members from the western provinces have somehow or other given the impression to


other hon. members of the house that we are crying blue ruin and are always asking for something which is unreasonable. I resent that suggestion very much. In the present crisis we do not want something that the rest of the people of Canada cannot and should not give. I am sorry that I was not a member of the house but was on the farm at the time the debate took place regarding the $65 million that was spent by the people of this country to reimburse the western farmers, but I have heard at least a dozen times since returning to the house that we gouged the treasury for $65 million.
I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will not object to my reminding him that he defended the cause of the western farmers on the ground that during the war years the price of their product was fixed at a figure that did not give them the cost of production. The minister, speaking on July 29, 1944, said as reported at page 5624 of Hansard:
I was careful to see that there was nothing In the bill which said that we were going to base any decision on the cost of production. The cost of production may be only a part of the consideration. I think it is possible the board might determine that the farmer should have considerably more than his cost of production because of some other experience he has had in order to get through the transitional period in a proper position.
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) who, I am very sorry to see, is unable to be with us, made a very good speech during that debate. It is to be found at page 1081 of Hansard of March 9, 1951. He placed on the record some figures that have been played around with in connection with the loss suffered by the wheat farmers because of the British wheat agreement. I am not going to take any time in arguing that if there had not been an international wheat agreement we would have been able to sell all our wheat during those years at the maximum class II price. However, the hon. member for Battle River gave a total figure of $431,676,000 as the alleged amount that the wheat farmers lost because of the wheat agreement, and I think that somewhere between that amount and the $65 million a figure could be set which would be fair.
But I think there can be no argument about the other figures that the hon. member for Battle River placed on the record. They have to do with the losses suffered by the farmers as the result of subsidizing Canadian consumers during the period from 1946 to 1949 inclusive. He gives totals of $34 million, $21 million, $65 million, $9 million and $6 million for the various years, or a grand total of $136 million. I do not think

there is any doubt about it that all the people of Canada enjoyed the benefit of having cheap bread all through that period at the expense of the farmers, who were obliged to buy their farm machinery at prices that were going up every day and every week. All the farmers of western Canada, regardless of their political views, feel that the $65 million voted by the government of the day was no handout but was a very niggardly settlement in payment of an obligation of all the taxpayers of Canada to a group that had produced wheat at low prices during the war and after the war.
After saying that, I admit very frankly that the situation at this time does present a most serious problem. I am not going to minimize it, and it is not likely that members of this group will be over on the government side in the immediate future and have the opportunity to solve it. But I want to outline some fundamental principles. I want to suggest that it should not be a serious problem for the Canadian people to do in peacetime what they did in wartime. The minister of finance of that time outlined the fiscal policy when he said that whatever is physically possible will be made financially possible. Since that was a good policy in wartime it is likewise a good policy in peacetime.
We really should not be concerned about having produced so much foodstuffs in the country that we do not know what to do about it. I want to emphasize again that those who live in industrial cities, those who are lawyers and storekeepers, are going to feel the impact of this trend very shortly. As a matter of fact the situation did not develop in the past week. It has been on our doorstep. It so happened that the government delayed action until near the end of the session. As an indication that these problems affect all of us, may I say that I note in the last weekly bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics that 78 per cent more commercial failures were recorded under the bankruptcy and winding-up acts in the first quarter of this year than in the first quarter of last year. The last issue of the Labour Gazette points out, as does the federation of agriculture, that farm income dropped 13 per cent in 1953 and was down 23 per cent in 1952. They draw our attention to the problem in the United States and point out that one union there reported
400.000	unemployed, that there are over
300.000	coal miners unemployed and 250,000 steelworkers. In the United States there are
950.000	listed as unemployed in three industries alone. In Canada that trend is going to develop. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr Howe) will agree, the farm implement industry workers, the automobile
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus workers and the textile workers have all been to Ottawa since we came here last November to place their problems before us and ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to take action.
Naturally, I am concerned about the problem of wheat and what we are going to do. I am indebted to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) for some words of wisdom he used when he spoke to the last annual meeting of the federation of agriculture. He said:
-any government-these days is in trouble with some of the people all of the time, most of the people some of the time, but not, I hope, with all of the people all of the time.
It seems to me that the people I have the honour of representing have been in trouble with the government all the time. The minister quoted from the poet Willa Cather, who said:
Life is hard for most people, and when it is easy, it is hardest of all.
After making that quotation, I guess the minister decided it probably was not very appropriate for the group to whom he was speaking, so he quickly added:
There are times, however, I must confess, when I find it difficult to accept that philosophy that a life of ease is really a life of hardship and vice versa.
The problem that is going to confront the wheat producers is a matter with which I feel the government of this country is going to have to deal. I happen to be in the position where all my worldly possessions, such as they are, are tied up in farmland and equipment. I do not want sympathy from this house or from anyone. If it is a decision that Canadian overseas markets will not absorb large quantities of wheat in the years to come, let us make that decision, but do not freeze the farmers out at this time of year. As the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) pointed out, last year on April 27 the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced that the initial price in 1953 for wheat would be not less than $1.40. He has been involved in some discussion during this debate, but he has not yet said what the price for wheat will be for the 1954-55 crop. He did say there would be an interim payment, but he did not say that all the wheat that is now on the western farms will be accepted at the present initial price and that there will be an interim payment on all the grain that has been grown in the year 1953.
Until the minister is prepared to make a further commitment on these two points, the fact that all the wheat grown last year will be accepted at the prevailing initial price and that there will be a further payment on

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus all the wheat grown last year, western farmers are going to be in a period of uncertainty. If the government decides that we are not going to be able to sell a large volume of grain, there is no point in western wheat producers trying to compete with the United States. But I suggest that is a decision the government could make, and that the government must make. Again I want to remind the house that twice during my lifetime a Conservative government and then a Liberal government came into the field to take over the marketing of the farmers' wheat during wartime. During the first world war the government stepped in and prevented wheat from going up to a probable $5 per bushel. During the second war when it appeared as though wheat were going up again, the government came into the picture and prevented the farmers from having all that the traffic would bear. Now that there is a large surplus of this product, I feel that the government cannot bail out without making some adjustment for the sins of commission in the past.
The Minister of Agriculture was good enough to refer to the position prevailing in the United States. I want to say again that I am happy I am living in Canada rather than in the United States. But I see no reason why our Department of Agriculture should not be willing to go as far in meeting the needs of the Canadian farmer as does the United States government. The United States government has this large surplus on hand, but they are in a different position. They can give all their surplus food away without having any serious repercussions on their own economy. This action would have a serious effect on our market, but we are not in that position. We export such a large percentage of our production that we cannot give away much without there being quite a drain on our economy.
We must face the facts. At the moment we have about four years' wheat supply for domestic consumption. At the end of the present crop year we will have about four years' supply of the total imports that the British would require. Well, with that situation I feel the Canadian government must look at the problem and must decide who are to take the consequences. I want to say to those who live in Ontario and Quebec that for 50 years it has been part of the policy of Canada to develop the great plains of the west on the theory that we would have overseas markets for unlimited quantities of grain. If that situation is changed, if European countries have now decided that as insurance against war they must increase their


own production, subsidize their own production and cut down their imports from abroad, that creates a problem that vitally affects every Canadian.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada, rather than the prairie wheat producers, should deal with this problem and should face the facts. In the United States they try to deal fairly with the farmer. One farmer has defined the parity price this way:
If you can sell a truckload of wheat and buy with the money as much food, clothing, building materials, farm machinery, fertilizer, and the like as you could in the five years, 1910-1914, your wheat is selling at the parity price.
That is all the farmers want. They want to be able to sell a truckload of wheat and buy the other commodities produced in Canada.
The Minister of Agriculture had a good deal to say about cutting down acreage. He may remember that during the war he asked the Canadian farmers to help win the war by growing less wheat, by cutting down their production.
And paid them for it.

Yes, and paid them for it. There is no reason why the Minister of Agriculture should not go to the farmers again and say, "We are sorry; we cannot use or sell all the wheat you have been growing. You have made your contribution to the Canadian economy, and we want to play fair with you." I submit that if Canadian farmers were able to get prices like the United States farmers of $2.18 a bushel, there is not a farmer of whom I know who would not be willing to drastically reduce his wheat acreage to get that sort of price. The weekly Searle grain report gives us the comparative prices for wheat, and shows that at Portal, North Dakota, the price was $2.13, whereas at North Portal, Saskatchewan, it was $1.43. I believe everybody will agree that the farmers south of the line buy their machinery at lower prices, as well as their gasoline and other commodities. Their operating costs are lower than in Canada.
May I say a word about the international situation? I feel we must face the fact that $2,000 million per year is a very large amount for Canada to be putting into our defence expenditures. I do not feel we can treat our farmers as has been proposed. It is inevitable that we have some soft spots in our economy if we are going to put such a large amount into national defence. The $2,000 million that we are putting into national defence is not, I think, giving us

the best results in this race in which we are engaged, in an effort to prevent the spread of communism.
Lord Boyd Orr said this:
The most urgent material need of the world today is food. Prolonged hunger causes social and political unrest, and hinders co-operation, not only between nations, but even within nations. Already the fear of another war casts its shadow on mankind. Statesmen are finding difficulties in laying the foundations of permanent world peace . . . But man and his governments have their eyes on the wrong goal. Hunger is at the heart of the world's troubles. Unless people are fed, the best treaties and agreements can come to nothing. Hungry people cannot be satisfied by anything but food.
I notice that recently in the American congress representative Wiley, chairman of the committee on foreign relations, said this about surpluses:
I do not view the C.C.C. stocks as an embarrassment to be disposed of as quietly and quickly as possible. I view them rather as assets . . . which we are lucky to have. They are also a challenge. Surely a people who can produce the hydrogen bomb has the ingenuity not to let butter spoil in government warehouses while some are hungry? It would be downright immoral to allow such a thing to happen. The conscience of the American people would not allow it.
They should devote more effort to utilizing this bounty, and less to penalizing its producers . . . Any other country in the world that was blessed with $350 million worth of dairy products would give thanks-not rap anybody's knuckles.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) suggested the other night that there are no longer any hungry people in the world, that nobody wants our wheat. But that is not the way we hear it from the food and agriculture organization. That organization tells us that a large group of mankind, more than a billion human beings, never get enough food for health, growth and full physical development. Those people are poor. Their food consists mainly of grain, starchy roots and tubers. These peoples are found in some parts of Africa, Europe and Central America. They may also be found in parts of the most prosperous countries, including our own.
So I think we can agree that, internationally, we should do everything within our power to see that surplus foods are made available to all who are hungry, and that in Canada no one should run short of food. It is pointed out in a newspaper report that an American sergeant gets as much pay as a French colonel. Maybe that does not create any problem for the American sergeant, but I do submit that it creates a problem for the French army. And it creates a problem for us at the present time, when we have such a high standard of living in this country, and yet seem to be unwilling as a people to share the excess.
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus
So I submit that in offering this amendment we are merely asking that all the people of Canada stand behind the wheat producers in this particular crisis.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
In the earlier part of his remarks the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) made a statement which conveyed the impression that on May 6, 1953, my colleagues and I -and he referred to me particularly-had voted in this house in favour of a C.C.F. amendment in terms similar to that now under debate.
I could not believe my ears, and sent for Hansard. I find that Hansard for May 6, 1953, at page 4857, gives the following as the text of the C.C.F. amendment then under debate on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply:
That all the words after the word "That" to the end of the question be struck out and the following words be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that consideration should be given to an increase of 25 cents in the initial payment for No. 1 Northern wheat basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver for the crop year beginning August 1, 1953, so that the said initial payment will be $1.65 per bushel."
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that I voted for that amendment, and it is also a fact that my Conservative colleagues voted for it. But it is not a fact, as the hon. member's words convey, that that amendment was of the same nature, for the same purpose or to the same effect as the amendment now under debate. On the contrary, it was of a very different nature. It related purely and simply to the amount of the initial payment for the crop year 1953-54. That is a far cry from a motion under which the C.C.F. now invite the house to subscribe to a policy of establishing a floor price of $1.82J per bushel indefinitely. The two things are quite different.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that there is nothing inconsistent in the position we took on May 6, 1953, in supporting a proposal for an increase in the initial price for the crop year 1953-54, and the position we now take against the present C.C.F. amendment. The two matters are quite different.
I wish to say emphatically that the impression that would have been created by the remarks of the hon. member in this respect is entirely misleading.

Mr. Speaker, I realize the house is ready to get on with other business-and rightly so-and I do not want to increase its restiveness to any degree at all. But since reference was made to me
6056	HOUSE OF
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus by my good neighbour to the south, the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) I think I would be lacking in courtesy if I did not say something at this time.
I appreciate very much his deep concern at my not having done credit to myself the other day, when I offered a few remarks. I wish to thank him for his concern and express the hope that as time goes on his estimation of me may improve.
In his speech the hon. member tried to indicate that my knowledge of the western farm situation was superficial, to say the least. He made special reference to what I had said about seeing the ships moving these millions of bushels of grain before my very eyes from Fort William, and suggested that my reference to that was indicative of the fact that I have only a superficial knowledge and appreciation of the difficulties we may be having in the west.
Unfortunately this is but another illustration of the methods so often employed by my friends in the C.C.F. out in our fair province of Saskatchewan. They will take one small illustration out of one's statement, as he has done with what I said the other day, and from it judge one's attitude on a situation. The hon. member did not refer to the fact that I had indicated that in Canada we are in a period of readjustment. He did not refer to the fact that we want as high a price as possible in western Canada for our grain. He did not refer to the fact that I said that if we had to take the lead in this economic adjustment taking place throughout the world in this post-war period, when we are entering into a competitive world market, we would expect an adjustment in the prices of the machinery which enters into the cost of production.
AH these salient facts I tried to point out in humble, perhaps not as parliamentary language as he can use, but nevertheless I expressed them at that time. He merely used that one expression of mine with respect to keeping these millions of bushels of grain moving. That sort of thing is not new to us out in Saskatchewan. We know that if there is any group of people who shy away from facts it is that group that is represented on the other side of the house; although I should inform the house that gradually reasonableness is beginning to assert itself, and more and more we find the members opposite from Saskatchewan drifting away from the actual feeling of the people who elected them. That was illustrated the other day when I quoted this pamphlet entitled "Saskatchewan Invites you", which is broadcast throughout the world by the Saskatchewan government at the international fair at Toronto.


As the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) said yesterday, we can expect these people to go north, and you can look for them in the south. Well, it so happens that the two divergent pictures presented by the party in Saskatchewan are both north and south. What we hear in the house is entirely different from the picture that is presented to Canada and the rest of the world by the officials of the Saskatchewan government.
For the information of the house, and for the information of the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough), I have had some connection with the growing of wheat, and also have been in touch with marketing agencies. As a matter of fact, when the wheat pool was first organized I, in my own little corner, did what I could in the organization in that area, and you will find a good many wheat pool contracts that I signed up some thirty years ago. I was with the wheat pool organization at that very critical time that was dealt with by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) yesterday. From 1929 to 1931 I was with the field service department of that organization, and it was my duty at that time to travel throughout the province from Lloydminster to the Manitoba boundary, and in a great many points throughout the province, explaining the difficulties that the wheat pool got into at that time with regard to the so-called overpayment when the price was raised beyond what conditions warranted.
I intended to deal with that period, but the Minister of Agriculture did it yesterday in a very much more able manner than I could. I mention that to show that it is not just a question of observing ships on lake Superior that indicates my general knowledge of and attitude toward conditions in the west. Then, too, I have known personally every one of the members of the present wheat board, because it so happens that all of them, with the exception of the last one, Mr. Robertson, who was added from the grain trade of western Canada recently, went through this experience of the period of the wheat pool together. Mr. Mclvor, Mr. McNamara, Mr. Riddel and Mr. Davidson; I knew all these people in 1929. They have had the experience of the ups and downs in marketing grain in the international markets of the world, and I do not think you will find anywhere in the world a more capable board to handle grain and to sell our grain than the wheat board as constituted at the present time.
Then, too, I have grown grain, or tried to grow it, in the hungry 1930's. No one needs to tell me just what the difficulties were. I sold rye for 11 cents a bushel. A few

years ago I sold rye for $3.85 a bushel. I did not hit the high of $4.11. It just goes to show that I have had some experience with the vagaries of the markets of the world with respect to making a living on a farm. So much for that.
I have tried to keep in touch with all of the municipalities in my riding, and this brings me to the point of the picture that is being given us by hon. members, which is at variance with the picture that is given us by the government of Saskatchewan in the publication I quoted the other day. I have kept in touch with all the municipalities in my constituency of Qu'Appelle even before I came down here. I wrote to them throughout the winter, asking them to bring any difficulties that they may have in which I could be of service. Well, I was able to be of some service in the distribution of box cars and so on, not that everything desired was done, but by simply pressing along for action. I do not say that I was any more successful than anyone else, but I have been in close touch with them.
The economic picture that is being presented, the picture of catastrophe and imminent collapse in western Canada alongside the picture that is being painted to us and to the rest of the world of this huge surplus that we have out there does not agree. What do hon. members think will be the effect upon our buyers and the rest of the world? On the one hand we are just on the brink of economic collapse, and on the other we have tremendous wheat surpluses. Will the buyers of wheat not be inclined to say that those fellows are just about at the end of their tether? These people are in the position where they are not able to carry on, and we shall be able to get that wheat cheaper. I would say that by the talk of the members opposite and by their actions they are helping to drive down the price of wheat in the world markets. I do not say that is the only factor. I do not give them credit for that much international influence, but I do insist that more harm has been done by this eternal talk of ruin, collapse and distress and about going back to the 1930's, than perhaps by any other factor in the markets of the world.
Those traders know how much wheat we have, but they do not always know the details of our local particular economic situation. But thanks to our friends opposite they are being enlightened to a very great degree. I think that is what is in the mind of the Saskatchewan government when it is trying to nullify, when it is trying to minimize, what we are being told by opposition members of the house.
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus
For some two months now a great deal has been said about the distressing conditions in the west, how we shall not be able to put in our crop for lack of funds, and the difficulty that we shall have in regard to operating our farms, and so on. When the Minister of Agriculture was premier of Saskatchewan, in the most distressing period that Saskatchewan ever went through, it was my privilege to serve under him. We had on the statute books legislation which provided government guarantees to municipalities to assist in putting in crops and helping with summer fallow, and so on. Last spring, when this talk was going on in the House of Commons by hon. members opposite, the Saskatchewan government, under the department of municipal affairs, at the head of which is my friend Mr. McIntosh, made a survey by means of a questionnaire in which it was attempted to summarize conditions and to focus the need for assistance to individuals in the municipalities of the province. I have a copy of the questionnaire here, which I obtained at Easter, and which went into it in some detail. Each councillor was asked to make a survey of conditions and this was to be used as a basis for action. Now, what happened? How widespread and acute was this distress? The other day I said there was a dollar shortage in the west. But that dollar shortage is due to the very same reasons which have resulted in a dollar shortage in eastern Canada. As soon as people are out of their jobs for three or four months and swell the ranks of the unemployed, then they have little cash to fall back upon for the very simple reason that they have spent most of the money they had earned.
We have had more money during the last three years than ever before and that is proven not by me but by the statistics which make it quite clear that while the farm cash income in the rest of Canada declined over the past two years, the whole of Saskatchewan farm cash income increased in 1953 from what it was in 1952 and prior to that; and indeed, the actual figure is $711-4 million for 1953.
The reason for the dollar shortage is obviously due to the fact that we have spent that money in paying our debts, buying machinery, and making other improvements, and while we may not have the money we have at least the value therefor. In the very same fashion, many a good business finds itself in difficulties because it has not got the ready cash, though it has good assets. Many of our people in both the west and the east are in much the same position. They have spent their money in buying automobiles, television, radios, homes

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus and other things, and once they are out of a job for two or three months they are in a difficult position. This is followed by requests that the government through the taxpayer of Canada should at once begin to employ 500,000 people. Now we are being asked to give the people in Saskatchewan some consideration, and I am all for it, provided the need is there.
Ever since 1935 this government has never left western Canada in the lurch. Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act many dams have been constructed to alleviate the distress which occurred in previous years; also the $65 million, which was referred to a short time ago, was provided by this parliament. I might add that it was not easy for hon. members of this parliament, particularly on this side of the house, to vote for this grant, because there was some doubt on the part of eastern and B. C. members at that time that we were fully entitled to this $65 million. But there was never a word of thanks from the other side of the house in this regard. On behalf of the people in the west I want to thank members of this house for taking the view that such a payment was necessary, and supporting the proposal so ably put forward by the Minister of Agriculture at that time. It was at some political sacrifice that some of the hon. members from eastern Canada voted for this measure because they found themselves in a very precarious position when they sought re-election, and some hon. members sacrificed their political lives to give us that $65 million. I wish to again thank the government and the Prime Minister for taking such a fair attitude toward the prairie farmer.
In regard to the present situation I might add that 1 am not the least bit concerned about the government coming to our aid when there is a real need. When we have to cry "wolf" I am quite sure the government will come to our rescue and give whatever assistance is possible. But this cry of "wolf, wolf" before the wolf has actually arrived is liable to bring about the same distress as that which was brought about in that old fable we all know so well.
I might point out that we in Saskatchewan have legislation fully capable of dealing with distress conditions such as have been pictured here by the opposition, but which have not yet arrived. The legislation to which I refer is the good Liberal legislation which is on the statute books of Saskatchewan at the present time. In this regard I would like to point out that Premier Douglas, speaking at the annual convention of the rural municipal association of Saskatchewan, dealt with this situation. I would like to quote his remarks as reported in the


News, of Wolseley, Saskatchewan, on Wednesday, June 2, 1954. The report reads as follows:
The Saskatchewan government will this year extend the provisions of the municipal seed grain and seed supply act to cover assistance to farmers on summerfallowing operations. Premier T. C. Douglas said in Regina Friday.
Speaking at the annual convention of the rural municipal secretary-treasurers' association of Saskatchewan, Mr. Douglas said municipal secretaries would soon be notified of the change.
The act provides for provincial guarantee of bank loans to municipalities, the money to be used to assist farmers to meet seeding costs.
"The government has made it clear that this assistance is again available this year and has decided to notify municipalities that.it is prepared to have the legislation apply to summerfallow as well as seeding," the premier said.
He said that, in the main, municipalities have not felt it was necessary to apply for aid under the act this year but the legislation is there for any municipality wishing to take advantage of it.
Reason for extending the act to cover summer-fallow expenses was the difficulty of marketing the 1953 crop, he said.
I would like to draw hon. members' attention to what follows:
Sales of wheat were beginning to pick up and the situation is more hopeful, he said, but it is not expected that the quota on deliveries will be raised above seven bushels an acre in this crop year which ends July 31.
In effect, Mr. Douglas is saying that the situation is more hopeful and that the grain is moving. Now, how can we reconcile that with the statements we have heard in this house? Premier Douglas was addressing one of the most responsible elected bodies we have in Saskatchewan, a body which is noted for its reasonableness in its approach to local as well as general problems affecting the west. It is sometimes called the unofficial parliament of Saskatchewan, and the reasonable people who comprise that body can be counted upon to give a true interpretation of what conditions really are.
Now, I do not wish to put facts and figures on the record with respect to the production or marketing of wheat because it has been my observation that facts and figures, particularly facts, can be marshalled and will not convince those they are intended to convince. You can build a granite pyramid of facts and it would have absolutely no effect on some people in this house. They are in much the same position, I am afraid, as that of the old gentleman who visited the zoo for the first time. I do not know what his political persuasion was, but he arrived at the cage in which the giraffe was installed. He had never seen a giraffe before. He looked at it; took off his glasses; rubbed his glasses, put them on again; looked at it again; folded his glasses up, put them in his pocket, and said: "I just do not believe it."

Some people in this house have the same attitude towards facts. I do not apply this to the people who elected some of our friends opposite in Saskatchewan because many of them are finding that reasonableness is catching up with them, and I might add that I have not a single personal enemy in that whole group. As a matter of fact, some of them voted for me. Indeed, if I may let a secret out, some of the Conservatives voted for me. They thought that I was a reasonable kind of guy. That is the general attitude there, namely one of reasonableness.
I want to draw attention to one or two attitudes relative to wheat marketing that perhaps have not been emphasized. The opposition is in a peculiar situation. They go to great pains to say that the record of the wheat board is all right. The Conservative group speaks a little bit gingerly about that system. In fact I noticed that here and there the gentlemen I admire very much, namely the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), touched upon the matter of the present system of wheat marketing a bit gingerly. But there are some people immediately opposite me who proclaim their adherence to the wheat board and yet at the same time try to condemn the government. They praise the wheat board for selling the wheat and condemn the government for not selling it. They praise the wheat board-[DOT] and here I will work in a figure or two- for selling wheat to 67 different countries of the world the year before last, for selling wheat to nearly 80 countries of the world last year, and for selling, in the year 1952-53, into the export markets of the world more wheat that did the United States during the same period. Of course those are facts. But some of my friends directly opposite-and I refer particularly to the members sitting in the house and not to the general membership of that party out in the country-when they have facts approach them, think they have something undesirable to deal with, and they will take hold of that fact and twist and contort it until that fact shrieks and screams for help. On the other hand, if there is a beautiful theory that approaches them- a theory all dressed up in "buttons and bows", they immediately lock arms and walk down the street with it. They love theories and they deplore facts. The more bold the fact is, the more is that fact to be challenged and demolished if possible. That situation comes about, of course, owing to the suspicious nature of some people. What I mean is this. Some things look so good-and that is the situation in connection with the marketing of grain up to the present time- that it is hard to believe them; they say there
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus must be something wrong; it cannot be that good, just as they say that about this wheat board report: sales cannot be that good. It took them by surprise. I think there are going to be some heart to heart talks among the C.C.F. I think perhaps the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is out in Saskatchewan right now trying to clear the matter up out in the west.
But I must not transgress any longer, Mr. Speaker. I have tried to remind the house that, as far as wheat is concerned, the wheat board is selling wheat. As far as the government is concerned, it is the policy of this government-as it was the policy of the pool when I was associated with it, with the exception of one unfortunate experience-to sell wheat wherever there is a possible market for it. How much plainer than that can you make a policy? It is the policy of this government to sell wheat. I say to my hon. friends: Read your wheat board report. If you do not believe it, I am sorry for you. I cannot help you, much as I should like to do so.
If we have to make a readjustment, well and good. I think most people are realizing that we may have to make a readjustment and that it will be good business to do so. A country of 15 million people-men, women and children-cannot possibly buy a billion bushels of wheat. I want to remind the house that the hon. member for Assiniboia said not a million, but he said: Canada should store up a billion bushels of wheat to have for sale. By the time the taxpayer buys a billion bushels of wheat and by the time he catches up with his defence program and by the time the taxpayer employs 500,000 unemployed from one end of this country to the other, we shall perhaps be arriving at the ultimate objective of a certain political group operating in this country and which says that, if we want a really modern society, we should have state ownership and state control of the means of production, distribution and exchange and that therein lies the solution of all the economic difficulties of the world. If these policies are pursued, taxation will be so great that we shall eventually as individuals have to hand over to the state-for the buying of wheat, for the hiring of people and for all these different things that have been mentioned- so much of all that we earn that we shall have arrived at that idealistic state where we will live a system of state ownership and control of the means of production, distribution and exchange. I do not think the Canadian people want that.
Of course my friends of the Social Credit party in the extreme corner of the chamber

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus to your left, Mr. Speaker, are very amiable gentlemen. But I do not see how they can hold some of the views they hold, considering what fine people they are. But whether we are dealing with wheat or whether we are dealing with any other problem, the solution inevitably brought forward by these people I look upon as unique. In many respects they agree with the rest of the people of Canada with respect to private enterprise as a main source of national wealth and so on, but they have one cure-all. That cure-all is illustrated in a story of many years ago, namely that of Aladdin and his lamp. As you will remember, Mr. Speaker, Aladdin was a young lad who found a lamp and by rubbing this lamp a genie would appear; he then could ask for anything that his heart desired and that would be added unto him. There is one thing that I have noticed and it is this. No matter what topic comes up for discussion, I almost know the last few paragraphs of every speech that comes from that corner of the house because they will proclaim this, which I call the Aladdin's lamp of finance. This Social Credit financial Aladdin's lamp theory is handed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and then all he has to do is to rub that lamp and purchasing power-a phrase so glibly used- is at once abundant to all, whether in this country or any other country, and in that way we solve our difficulties. I wish the solution were that easy. I think the emblem that our friends should have or the badge that they should wear is a very simple one, namely this Aladdin's lamp which they could wear in their buttonholes, thus identifying themselves with this Utopian approach to all the difficulties of the world.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I have taken so long at this time-
And so are we.

-but I felt that I wanted to put forward a few explanations in view of the fact that I have been referred to upon several occasions. I apologize to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the other members who are anxious to get on with the business for taking so long.
That is the most sensible thing the hon. member has said.
However, I wanted to put these few observations on the record.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some hesitancy that I rise because it seems that the motion which was introduced yesterday has come to be regarded by the hon. members on both sides of the house at the south


end as a declaration of private war between the members for Saskatchewan on both sides of this house. It is perfectly true that occasionally, just so that it might not be regarded as too exclusive a war, there has been a very limited reference to the Conservative party in connection with this matter. That, however, was only a gesture of respect rather than any indication that the war was ceasing to be a private war. I do wish to get back to the basic discussion that we have before us, and I have no doubt that this private war will continue outside with the same vigour and refreshing references to ancient history that have characterized it both yesterday and today. Aladdin now joins Demosthenes in dealing with the problem of western wheat. Nevertheless, I would prefer that we come back to the immediate problem presented by the somewhat impressive reality that we are now just six weeks away from the beginning of a new crop year.
We are also confronted with the inescapable fact that we have an unprecedented surplus of wheat. We are confronted with the fact that we have an unprecedented accumulation of wheat on the farms. We are confronted with the fact that on the basis of present sales the accumulation now on the farms is going to be nothing compared with the accumulation there will be in the coming crop year unless something is done which has in no way been indicated to the hon. members of this house.
This is a particularly appropriate time to discuss this subject even though our simple resolution which declared the desire that there be a statement of policy has led to this private war from which I am now seeking to bring the house back at least for a time. I would point out that there is a special reason why this subject is of great and urgent importance in addition to the reality of the threat with which the farmers of western Canada are confronted. That is the fact that the 47-nation international wheat council, which has been described in dispatches as the parliament of the international wheat agreement, assembled this morning in London. This international parliament, which determines various problems under the international wheat agreement, is now at this very moment discussing in London matters of immense importance to the wheat producers of Canada.
When I directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few days ago with regard to the representation that Canada would have at that 47-nation meeting in London and the instructions which would be given, we were told that of course the wheat

board is an independent body. I must confess, whatever the criticism I may direct to the minister at any time, that he has not shown himself unaware of the details of the operation of the wheat board on ordinary occasions. I also have not found a reluctance on the part of the government to indicate some measure of satisfaction as to the part it has played in the operation of the wheat board, when that was convenient. It can of course be very convenient to cloak it with an atmosphere of independence that not one of us really believes it has. In fact it is only necessary to go back to the figures of forced sales just prior to the election last year to realize how unreal that cloak of independence really is. Nevertheless we can dispense with that.
We are confronted with the reality of this immense surplus. We are confronted with the fact that we are within six weeks of the new crop year. We are confronted with the fact that the farmers of western Canada have no statement from the government to guide them in planning for that new crop year. That applies not only to the farmers but also to the merchants, to those who will be handling the grain, to the railway companies and the shippers of the grain to distant points.
I am not suggesting that the difficulties confronting the government and wheat producers generally are not immense. We all know that there is a world problem emerging. Nevertheless this very government has boasted over and over again of the extent to which it has been willing to intervene with respect to various aspects of production. In fact it has on the statute books now wide open powers which permit it to intervene. It has claimed credit where that intervention was for good. Let it not deny its responsibility to intervene when we are confronted with a situation which in fairness we must concede is now on a world-wide scale. That is the subject that is being discussed in London at this moment by the 47-nation conference meeting there. Not only the house but the farmers of Canada should be informed what instructions the Canadian representatives at that meeting have been given.
Does the minister suggest for one moment that what has been described as the parliament of the international wheat agreement has Canadian representatives attending that parliament with not a hint of instructions from the government of Canada? There is not a member of the house who will believe for a moment that such is the situation. Most certainly some advice, some instructions, some indications, have been given, and it would be helpful to us to know what they are. Let
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus us not have the answer that these are discussions which should not be rigid in advance. Of course they should not be rigid in advance. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) nevertheless did not hesitate to state to us certain aspects of Canadian policy at the time the Geneva conference was meeting. In fact he stated certain aspects of our policy on an earlier occasion before the conference even met. Here we have a very practical conference to deal with the problem of the world marketing of wheat under the international wheat agreement and there is more reason for giving us information because this is a business problem without some of those secret connotations of international discussions such as are taking place at Geneva.
It would be helpful to us and appropriate to know what the view of the government is with regard to these discussions and at least what they hope to attain at the conference even though their hopes may not be fulfilled. I also want to point out with reference to the remarks that have just been made that we are not touching this subject gingerly in any way. You know, I must admit there are some members of the Liberal party for whose opinion I have an increasing regard, but nevertheless they have absorbed the folklore of Liberalism without any of the corrective influences that would be presented by an opportunity to discuss some of the realities of history with them. In fact there are Liberals opposite who even seem to think that the wheat board is the product of the unlimited genius of the men opposite who have been extolled in such warm terms in the remarks we heard a short time ago.
Need it be recalled, just to deal with some aspects of his folklore of Liberalism, that it was the Bennett government that created the wheat board. In fact, while we do not always agree with the statements of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), it may be wise, in dispelling some of the visionary aspects of that folklore, to recall the simple, direct statement made by the Minister of Agriculture as recently as June 15, 1954, only yesterday, when he said, as found at page 6035 of Hansard:
The government of Mr. Bennett brought down a bill to provide for the compulsory marketing of western grain through a wheat board.

The legislation, Mr. Speaker, was introduced, and the legislation was the legislation which was carried forward by

I admit this government did withdraw some of the rather good features of it. Nevertheless, the basic features were retained. This government brought it under government control and did not give that measure of representation to the farmers themselves that was in the original concept of that board as presented by the Bennett government.

May I suggest that if we are going to have another private war at this end between the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), they carry it on between themselves. I accept the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture that the government of Mr. Bennett brought down a bill to provide for the compulsory marketing of western grain through the wheat board.

As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I said I was referring to a small statement made by the minister, and I am not going to read it all because everybody knows the Minister of Agriculture does not make short statements. I am not going to read the whole of this rambling statement. I have referred to this statement about the wheat board, and it is clear. Let me read this, however, from page 6035 of Hansard for June 15, 1954:
I must say, to the credit of the Bennett government of that day, that they brought down a bill which provided not only for compulsory marketing of wheat but compulsory marketing of all grain.
But they did not pass it; go on and read it.

We have heard the Minister of Agriculture on this subject many times, and undoubtedly he will be on it many times again. He has an opportunity to say what he likes, but surely he will not be critical if for once we take his words and accept them in their exact meaning. Incidentally, on this occasion they are clear and understandable.
May I just recall to the Minister of Agriculture that touching picture he once gave us of the three who sit together, and his words that Canada never needs to worry as long as these three hon. gentlemen are still here.
Hear, hear.

The applause from the other side, Mr. Speaker, will indicate that the other members commend that situation in which the members abdicate their responsibility and leave with these three hon. gentlemen the supreme authority over the affairs of their party. Nevertheless, I would recall that on that occasion the thing that prompted these very modest remarks by the Minister of Agriculture, in which he said that as long as he and the other two were there everything would be all right, was the fact that there had been a definite difference of opinion expressed by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This difference was resolved by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). It was the resolving of this difference that prompted the Minister of Agriculture to tell us all that, whatever difference might develop within that triumvirate, as long as the difference could be resolved by the Prime Minister all would be well in this difficult world.
The fact remains that we have something of the same kind today. I leave it there. If this private war is going to take place between the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Minister of Agriculture, then, let it take place. I simply want to point out, referring back to the folklore of Liberalism which I have mentioned, that we have the words of the Minister of Agriculture which indicate the extent to which there has been agreement in regard to the place of the wheat board. There has been agreement in regard to methods; there has been agreement in regard to the services that it has performed. So far as I am aware, that agreement extends into every part of this house.
One of the features in regard to the operation of that wheat board has been that, instead of a fixed floor price of the nature contemplated by the subamendment now proposed by the-

-C.C.F. party-I must admit that the names become transposed at times, and I do not know whether to call it the Liberal-Socialist or the Socialist-Liberal party, but we will call it the C.C.F. party. In regard to the C.C.F. party subamendment, may I point out that it refers to a fixed price which, under the situation that now exists, is unrealistic. This house, including the members of the C.C.F., have accepted a method of operation under the wheat board by which an initial price would be announced. It is true that that substantially had the effect of establishing a floor price. What we have pointed out is that for some years past

that initial price has been announced prior to the seeding in the spring. It has been announced at a time which made it possible for the farmers to know where they were. It has been announced at a time that helped, in some measure, the planning of operations on the farm during that year.
It has been pointed out, and I think bears repeating, that in 1950, for the 1950-51 crop year, the initial price was announced on April 5. In 1951, for the 1951-52 crop year, it was announced on May 4. In 1952, for the 1952-53 crop year, it was announced on April 8. In 1953, for the 1953-54 crop year, it was announced on April 27. This is June 16, and that initial price has not yet been announced. It is in relation to that fact, Mr. Speaker, and to the general absence of any statement which indicates that the government is dealing with that problem, that we have brought forward our amendment. We believe it states something that the house can support and should support, and that is the need for some action by this government to deal with this situation.
We believe that one of the essential steps is to follow out this earlier practice, even at this late date. We believe that, without another day's delay, the initial price should be set. Please let us hope we are not going to have a statement by the government that the independent body, the wheat board, still has not notified them. We know of the compelling arguments that are presented to the wheat board by the government in regard to matters of that kind. We have the evidence of it. We know quite well the government is in a position to announce, as the minister has announced over and over again in the past, this initial price. It should be done, and without further delay.
An added reason why it should be done is that we are confronted with a situation very similar to that facing farmers of the United States, but very unlike their situation in other ways. One thing that undoubtedly causes difficulty in the minds of the western farmers is the extent to which the land that is so similar, north of the border, grows similar crops under very dissimilar arrangements. In the United States the price paid is $2.21 per bushel under the arrangement which they have. There is something more, however, which we should not ignore. There is a limitation of crop production which our farmers have shown no willingness and no desire to accept. These are realities. I am simply making a statement of the situation that indicates why it is so essential that we have a clear statement of Canadian policy
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus and that we should not be just hanging on to the coat-tails of Uncle Sam at this time. Our position is different; the position of our farmers is different. The farmers of the United States do not feel the direct impact of these reductions in prices in the way it is felt by Canadian farmers. If there are to be further reductions, such as were at least contemplated in the statement made the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), then let us remember that it will be the Canadian farmer who will feel the direct impact of those reductions.
These are all reasons why there should be some action now which will give to our farmers and to those who are associated with them-to the servicing organizations and the transportation organizations both by rail and water and otherwise-some knowledge of what they may expect, and particularly in this new crop year which begins just six weeks from now.
Before closing my remarks may I refer to words that were spoken a few moments ago by the hon. member who preceded me in the debate. He reiterated a suggestion that has come from the other side of the house, including the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that this discussion should not take place because it is actually, in itself, harming our agricultural producers.
I do not question the hon. member's sincerity. Of course he was simply following members of the government in what he said-that "by their very action members on the other side are helping to drive down the price of wheat in the world market." I will admit that the remark was directed particularly to those who have been taking part in the private war. Nevertheless that remark had general application-"by their very action they are helping to drive down the price of wheat in the world market."
Then he did go on to make an observation which is very obvious. He said, "These traders know how much wheat we have". Of course they do. They are experts. They know how much wheat the department has, because that is their business. And then he said-and this is the remark upon which I place the greatest emphasis-"but they do not have the details of our economic position".
The hon. member has gone too far; he was carried away by his imagination. After all, why are the trade departments of all the embassies of the different countries established here in Canada, except to give those countries economic information about Canadian affairs? Do you not suppose they read every day the financial pages of our

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus newspapers? Do you not think they read the trade reports issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce? Do you not think they read the excellent financial and economic comments produced regularly by the banks? Of course they do.
The fact is that those governments, and the traders operating under them, are fully informed in regard to the details of our economic position. And do not let anyone suggest for a moment that our friends beyond the iron curtain are not equally well informed on this subject, in case their position might be affected in any way by this matter.
No, Mr. Speaker, the facts are before the traders of the world, whether they be government traders or private traders. The facts are before the people of Canada to the extent that our people take advantage of the information available. But one thing that is not before us is what this government is going to do to deal with that situation. Admittedly they cannot adopt an inflexible or utterly unreasoning rigidity in the face of the world situation with which we are confronted, and which does present them with grave problems and difficulties.
May I say this-and in saying it I am sure others on both sides of the house join with me-that, whatever our political differences may be, we want our government to tackle this problem in a way that will be best for the farmers of Canada and best for Canadians generally. And we wish them well in the great task they have before them in dealing with this immensely important problem.
Mr. Speaker, the realities cannot be escaped. We have an unprecedented surplus. Our farmers are confronted with uncertainties. And they are confronted with strained credit problems, until there is a clear statement. The first urgent step is the declaration of an initial price. Beyond that is at least a statement as to the things that this government hopes to achieve through this parliament, under the international wheat board now meeting in London, and by their own action in the markets of the world.
To such extent as they are prepared to take us into their confidence we will certainly co-operate with them in every way we can. To such extent as they can assist and guide our farmers and our producers and our servicing organizations, I am sure they will receive their co-operation.
This is a problem affecting the whole of Canada. It must be dealt with in the interests of all Canadians. That is the purpose of our amendment, and that is the reason we have placed it before the house. For the reasons

we have given we cannot support the subamendment. It is not dealing with the principle of floor prices. This marketing by the wheat board is something that has been accepted by all members of the house. The initial price is part of the accepted practice. You have had that initial price. We need no such subamendment as this, following the practice that has been adopted. And that is why we place before you a motion calling for action by the government at a time when action is so greatly needed.
