I want to quote his exact words because the hon. member complained this morning that what he had said had been misinterpreted. Here is what he said as reported at page 5793 of Hansard for June 10, 1954:
It so happens that we in western Canada are leading the way in this readjustment by having our prices come down.
Well, that is a very strange approach from a member who represents a wheat-growing area. But coupled with that, the whole tenor of his speech was that we cannot expect to hold the price at the level which our amendment suggests.
Now, in what position does that place the farmer? The fact is that over the years this government has asked the wheat growers of Canada to accept a lower price than the actual world market price at that time, and for the purpose of stabilization, as they called it during the war years. They said it was a matter of patriotic duty to produce and provide food for our allies. The farmers were told that their contribution, their sacrifice, if you will, was part of the national war effort and that the government would see to it that they were not left in the lurch, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said, after the war years. In order that that statement may not be challenged, let me give the exact words of the then prime minister of Canada. Speaking over the radio on December 4, 1943, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King said:
If to help win the war the farmers are asked to accept ceiling prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to assure them against an agricultural depression after the war.
Now, those are the words of the then prime minister of Canada in 1943, and they can be interpreted as nothing other than a direct promise that in compensation, or shall we say in appreciation of the sacrifices and the contribution the farmers were being called upon to make in order to assist the war effort in 1933, and subsequently, this government-or any other government, because I believe any prime minister who speaks on behalf of the nation speaks not only for the government of which he happens to be the head but for any other government which may subsequently follow-in return for that contribution in the interests of stabilization the farmers were to receive the floor price after the war years.
[Mr. Zaplitny.l

Now, it may be argued that they have a floor price in the sense that we have an initial price which is to be announced in the future, though we do not know when. But the question which comes up is whether the farmers are going to receive an adequate floor price which will compensate them or which will at least help them maintain their position in relation to the general price level in Canada. That is why I was so concerned when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said that we were leading the way in the price readjustment. Unfortunately it seems to me that no one is following that lead in Canada though it appears the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is quite satisfied that the wheat farmers shall be the ones to cut the prices of their products, perhaps as an example of what can be done in order to bring about an over-all downward price readjustment.
But who is following the lead? Let me refer to some other figures, and this is still within the purview of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I have some figures here which I have taken from the dominion bureau of statistics which show some of the prices of the manufacturing industries in Canada. Let us see whether they are taking part in this downward readjustment in which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is suggesting the farmers take the lead.
For example, taking the 26 major manufacturing industries in Canada-I could place all the categories on the record, but to save time I will not-it will be shown that for the year 1951 their net earnings were $1,548,300,000 compared with $1,005,200,000 in the average period 1946-50. This is an increase of over $500 million. Now, their profit, based on sales, averaged out in 1951 to 10-1 per cent, while during the period 1946-50 their average was only 9-7 per cent. The readjustment seems to be going forward, the prices are still rising and the trend is upward. Despite that, here we are being offered the recommendation that the wheat growers should lead the way in the readjustment downward. Where does that leave the farmer?
Let us take the profit on the basis of net worth, which I think is a better method of determining how they are doing. On the basis of their net worth, these 26 major manufacturing industries in 1951 made an average profit of 24-6 per cent. I give that figure because in a moment I am going to give some comparable figures in relation to the agricultural industry.
Perhaps it might be said that lumping all these industries together will not give a fair

sample, but in order that hon. members may not think so I am going to deal with some of the industries of which I have been talking, and I can give them all if necessary.
For example, starting with one which is supposed to be in a depressed position at the present time, namely, cotton textiles, their net earnings in 1951 amounted to $30-1 million, which represents a profit on sales of 9 [DOT] 8 per cent on their net worth or investment of 22-4 per cent. For the farm machinery companies there was a net earning of $38-1 million and a sales profit of 11 per cent on a net worth of 28-4 per cent. The petroleum refining industry had net earnings of $72,500,000, sales profit of 8 per cent, and on net worth of 14-3 per cent. The iron and steel industry had net earnings of $76-8 million, sales profit of 11-8 per cent, and on net worth of 25-1 per cent. The electrical equipment industry, which has been complaining for the last couple of years about lack of business, had net earnings of $72-5 million, sales profit of 9 per cent on a net worth of 27-8 per cent.
Now I come to pulp and paper, and might I just interject here that if the philosophy of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were followed by the pulp and paper industry they might not have been so well. The minister objected to discussion between Canada and the United States on a price being set under wheat, and he characterized that as the setting up of a combine. But recent events as related in the newspapers show that the pulp and paper business was not averse to setting up a combine with the result that in 1951 it did rather well with a net earning of $317 million which on sales amounted to 23-4 per cent and on their net worth amounted to 34-2 per cent.
Then, coming to the automobile and parts industry, the net earnings here amounted to $87 [DOT] 9 million on sales of 9-6 per cent on a net worth of 47-1 per cent, so that they have done rather well and their readjustment has been upward from the period 1946-50. While I have not figures for 1953, because they are not yet available, I have no doubt that they are still doing very well.
I have given these profits as based on their net worth in order that we may make a comparison with the agricultural industry. I have here in my hand a publication which I believe will be accepted as authoritative. It is published by the department of political economy of the University of Manitoba, and it contains a study which was made in the Birtle-Shoal Lake area of Manitoba. The Minister of Agriculture will be familiar with
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus that area and I think he will agree that it is fairly representative of that province. The farm lands in that area are not the best in the province and they certainly are not the worst in the province. They may be accepted as being the average type of land in the province. Perhaps for that very reason they were taken by this department for the purpose of making a study. It included 78 farms which ranged in size from a half-section to in some cases five quarters or more in one unit. A study was made covering production expenses, income and so forth. Let me just give a summary to show what the finding of this department was on that question. Incidentally this was published in November of 1953, so it is quite recent. It was found that on these 78 farms the average capital investment-that is including land, farm machinery, et cetera-was $15,896; the average cash income was $4,756 and the average current expense for each year was $2,007. That leaves an average net income of $2,749 per farmer. If we allow the very reasonable figure of $2,000 as wages to the farmer-because there is nothing here included so far which would pay wages to the man who operates the farm-we find a net return of $749 on the capital investment of $15,896. If we do that percentagewise, we find that it is a percentage of net worth of 4-7 per cent. Let me come back to some of these other figures and compare them-
Go back to Tommy Douglas's figures. They are more important.
I would appreciate hearing what the hon. member has to say.
I say: Go back to Tommy Douglas's figures.

I am afraid that the hon. gentleman was not listening because I have already said that these figures were prepared and published by the department of political economy of the University of Manitoba. They were published in November, 1953.
He does not understand.
I think it is a quite authentic and independent source and that there are no political implications here.
That is fine.

As I say, that is a return on a net worth for these 78 farms representing I think the average in Manitoba of 4-7 per cent as compared with the automobile industry with 47-1 per cent, as compared with the pulp and paper industry with 32-2 per cent or as compared with the petroleum industry

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus with 14-3 per cent or the farm machinery industry with 28-4 per cent, and so forth. I think that sets out quite clearly the fact that the farmers so far have not been receiving their fair share of the national income. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) has already stated that, in spite of the fact that the farmers represent approximately 20 per cent of the population in Canada, their share of the national income has been running, as most recent figures indicate, just slightly over 8 per cent. Taking all that into consideration, I do not believe it is at all unreasonable for this party or any party in this house to move that an adequate floor price be set under our basic commodity, namely wheat.
The Minister of Agriculture has given us in his usual delightful fashion a description of a meeting to which he spoke recently. I did not quite clearly catch where this meeting was, but anyway he said that the loudspeakers covered an area of 40 acres, that there must have been a large mass of people to occupy that area, and that after he had finished speaking and stated government policy on wheat he was told that he was dead right. Let me give the other side of the coin, shall we say. I have here a letter which I believe was received by every member of this house, dated June 15, from the Manitoba farmers union, who represent a large proportion of the farmers in Manitoba. No doubt their opinions will be the same as those of the Saskatchewan farmers union or of the farmers union in Alberta. Here is what they have to say. I wonder whether this will ring as if he was "dead right" according to the minister's statement. I quote from the letter:
The statement made recently by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe that the government is prepared to cut our wheat price again it necessary, was a shock to many western farmers, especially when it appears that the government is not prepared* to take any responsibility in the matter. It will be hard for western farmers to believe that the government expects them to compete with the U.S. treasury.
During the past two years, farm income dropped 23 per cent and this, coupled with the fact that while 20 per cent of the total Canadian population are engaged in agriculture they only receive 8'7 per cent of the national income, makes the outlook very serious for farm families. Recently farmers were forced to take another blow when the government slashed the price of wheat (by 17 cents per bushel in the past four months) -
That is apparently taking the 7 cent drop together with the 10| drop more recently. The letter continues:
-and is apparently prepared to go still further.
We are beginning to wonder how long it will take our government to realize that this will ruin western agriculture? During the war years we were told that our prices would be stabilized for the future-

And then follows the quotation from the prime minister of that day which I have already placed on the record. Then they follow that up by saying this:
What has happened to this promise? We still have the same government in power today, and the farmers feel that when a promise is made it should be maintained.
That is the opinion of a large body of farmers in my province.
If the hon. member will permit me to do so, I should like to make an interjection.
Yes.

I do not want to enter into the argument as to whether the floor that is on wheat is high enough or not, but I want to say to the hon. member that the quotation he has made has no bearing whatsoever upon that question. The quotation he has made does not apply because wheat is about the only farm product upon which there was not a ceiling during the war time.

That is an example of the type of interjection the Minister of Agriculture likes to make. But will he not agree with me to this extent? Will he not agree that it was the expressed policy of the government in 1943 that they were going to work towards the stabilization of the prices of farm products? The minister nods his head. I understand that nod means yes.

My hon. friend has not yet got the point. That statement which he has read-and which he is quoting and which he says the farmers union quoted-says that because there was a ceiling price put on certain products, there should therefore be a stabilization by putting on a floor price afterwards. Wheat is one product which that does not apply to. There was no ceiling on wheat during the period of the war.
Oh, yes, Mr. Speaker; it is true that that did not apply in 1943. But the minister certainly will not make the statement that that was true in 1946, 1947 or 1948.
The hon. member has not yet got the point. There was no ceiling on the wheat price until 1945 when the war was ended.

I thank the minister. That is not what I am drawing to the minister's attention. What he has said may be said to apply as of December 4, 1943, when the former Prime Minister made his statement, but it cannot be said to apply from 1945 on because a price ceiling was imposed.

You have not yet got the point. The statement you have read was to the effect that if we kept the price down

during the war we ought to hold the price level after the war. This is one product on which this was not done during the war.

Nonetheless the government in 1943 sold the farmers on the idea that if they would be satisfied to accept a lower price for their farm products during that period in the interests of stabilization the government would see to it that they would not lose in the post-war years because of having accepted such prices.
I am quite prepared to follow your argument and to agree somewhat with it. I am only pointing out to you that you are quoting something which does not apply to wheat.
I agree, so far as the ceiling on wheat is concerned, that it did not apply until 1945, but it did apply in subsequent years. I think we can agree on that.
The statement read "could not apply after 1945". The war ended in 1945 and there was no ceiling on wheat.

No; but under the British wheat agreement a ceiling was placed on wheat after the war ended. I think the minister will agree with that. I was about to point out that I believe it is a reasonable proposition for this party to ask at this time that an adequate floor price be placed under wheat. I want to be perfectly fair about the matter. There may be some difference of opinion as to what that price should be, and I was anxious to see at least one member from the Liberal ranks or a minister of the government rise in his place and say: The price you are suggesting is too high; we would suggest that a lower price, such and such a price, would be suitable. But that is not the basis on which they oppose the subamendment. They attack the subamendment on the basis that this parliament has no right to set a floor price under wheat, that it might mean subsidization. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) made the statement that the farmers did not want their product to be subsidized.

Mr. Speaker, I said no such thing. I think what I said was exactly the opposite, that we believe that the principle of the Agricultural Prices Support Act should be applied to wheat and that it should be applied in such a way that the farmers will be assured of getting their fair share of the national income, even if it does mean subsidization. I made it as plain as two and two make four. My hon. friend has no right to misrepresent my argument in the house.

If I did not state correctly what the hon. member said I am quite prepared to accept his correction. I do so quite gladly because now we know that at least the hon. member for Rosthern agrees that, if necessary, the farmers' products should be subsidized by the nation. I think we agree on that point. I agree with him completely, and that is an excellent reason why he should vote for the subamendment.
I have more faith in this government than I would have in that outfit over there.

I do not wish to interfere in any way with the faith of my hon. friend. I am quite happy to leave it to him. But the point I am getting at is that if the hon. member for Rosthern and some of his colleagues from Saskatchewan, Manitoba or elsewhere agree with us that, if necessary, wheat should be subsidized by the nation, that is a clear reason why they should support the subamendment. Some hon. members express a certain fear on the question of subsidization. I have heard that fear expressed in the house on more than one occasion. They say that the government will never agree to having the taxpayers subsidize the production of wheat. Members of the Progressive Conservative party have stated that they do not believe in the subsidizing of farm products, particularly wheat. If they wish to use that argument then they will have to go a little further and say that they also disagree with the subsidizing of gold production, which is a pretty costly proposition these days. Comparing the usefulness of gold and wheat, I see a much poorer case for the subsidizing of gold. I have always taken the position that if we continue to subsidize gold instead of food we will wind up with a mouthful of gold teeth and nothing to -chew on.
These hon. members would also have to oppose the subsidizing of the -coal industry, which runs into substantial figures. They would have to oppose the subsidizing of the steel industry, which in the past has run into substantial figures. They would have to oppose the whole tariff structure of Canada, which is one great complicated form of subsidization-that is all it is. All the manufacturing industries that enjoy such high protection are in effect being subsidized by the consumers of Canada. As I pointed out a few moments ago, the automobile industry enjoyed a profit of $87-9 million in 1951 which represents 47-1 per cent on their net worth. A good part of that large profit is in

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus the form of a subsidy paid by the Canadian consumer as the result of the tariff protection enjoyed by this industry. The tariff structure constitutes one of the biggest forms of subsidy in the country.
Therefore in order to be logical and to follow their beliefs through to a logical conclusion, all those who oppose the idea of the subsidizing of farm products would have to be equally opposed to every form of subsidization existing in the case of other industries and would have to favour the complete abolition of our whole tariff structure. Are they prepared to do that? I do not think there are many members of the house who would be prepared to go that far. They would say: No, we must maintain these forms of protection and subsidy in order to make sure that these industries have a fair chance to exist.
If that is the argument they wish to use, then I will go along with them and say: Let us extend that to cover agriculture and see to it that the production of basic commodities, the production of food, grain, livestock and other things, is put on a sound basis through a system of floor prices in order that stabilization of farm income may be assured. That is not asking too much. But when we propose that, what happens? I rather hesitate to get into what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) called the private war. Yet I feel that I must protest against certain statements made by the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) yesterday which I resented very much. I did not wish to add to the confusion at that time by rising to my feet and asking him to withdraw. As reported at page 6008 of Hansard of yesterday, he said:
What I wish to say. Mr. Speaker, is that that is the situation with socialists generally; that is the trouble we have internationally, because you cannot make agreements with these people. They do not keep their half of the agreement. Possibly, if we got rid of that type of thinking in the world we would not be faced with this debate now.
That is a most astounding statement to be made by a supposedly responsible member of the house. We have been told that some of the things said on both sides of the house may have the effect of making the selling of our grain more difficult. I can imagine nothing that could make things more difficult for this nation to trade with the other nations of the world than a statement of that kind. The hon. member says that internationally agreements cannot be made with socialist countries because they do not keep their word. Does the hon. member realize the implications of a statement of that kind? Not many years ago there was a socialist government in Great Britain which did a great deal


more business with this country than their present government is doing. I am not saying that in criticism of the present government but it is a fact that they did a great deal of business with Canada for which both Canada and Great Britain were thankful.
You have the socialist governments of the Scandinavian countries. There were socialist governments in Australia and New Zealand. All of them have done business with Canada, and for a member of the Liberal party to stand up and say that we cannot deal with socialists because they do not keep their agreements will, in my opinion, do more harm in the international sphere, so far as Canadian trade is concerned, than anything which has been said in the house. I deplore that very much. If the hon. member is opposed to the amendment which we are proposing, and if he thinks it is unnecessary to place a floor price under wheat; if he is opposed to subsidization, if necessary, of food products, then I am quite prepared to hear his arguments. But when he attacks this party and attacks socialist governments generally all over the world-it may not be long before we may have a lot more socialist governments than now exist with whom we have to trade-then he is doing this country a great disservice. He is prejudicing our approach to these nations on the basis of good faith. I hope we shall not hear any more remarks of this type in this debate.
I may point out that the hon. member for Meadow Lake, who was so critical about the alleged inaccuracy of members in this house, made a statement in that same speech that the present government has reduced the national debt. Of course, he immediately amended that by saying that was in the nonwar years. I would refer him to page 1059 of the Canada Year Book for 1953. There he will find the national debt for 1945 listed at $15,700 million; for 1952 it was $17,252 million, which covers those seven non-war years. The increase shown is about $2 billion. Now, when a member can be $2 billion out in his statements, he certainly should not be critical of the alleged inaccuracy of other members.
In conclusion, I want to say this. We are proposing this amendment in good faith. We hope the members of this house on both sides will accept the principle of a floor price under wheat as a matter of national interest, not because we are pleading any special favours for the farmers, not because we are pleading poverty of the farmers, but because we believe that, in the interests of stabilization of the greatest and basic industry in Canada, the house should adopt this motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

speechtext:
I declare the amendment lost. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the main motion?


Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.

Meteorological division-
489. Administration, operation and maintenance. $6,963,110.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, this item is for the administration, operation and maintenance of the meteorological division and the total vote amounts to about $7 million for the present fiscal year. This is an increase of nearly $500,000 over last year's vote. I notice in the details at page 549 there are increases in such items as freight, express and cartage of about $40,000; in facsimile communications, an increase of $125,000; teletype an increase of $30,000; publication of "monthly record of meteorological observations" and other papers, an increase of about $20,000; and for office stationery, supplies and equipment quite a large increase of $85,000 for this year over last.
Will the minister explain why it is necessary to have this very large increase in this item for the present year? Will he also give us some idea of the present situation with regard to weather mapping in Canada which, I presume, comes under this vote? I believe we have a very efficient system. Perhaps the minister could give the committee a short summary of the present situation.

This is, in fact, a large vote and there is, as my hon. friend says, an increase for which I think I can give a satisfactory explanation. In the first place, there is an increase of almost $500,000 in salaries which in itself accounts for a large portion of the increase to which my hon. friend refers. There is an increase of $125,000 with reference to facsimile communication, as he has pointed out, and that is for the new system of facsimile weather mapping introduced last year based at Dorval. It is a rather technical thing and I doubt if I can explain it fully, but the object of it is to centralize in one area our entire map analysis. In other words, the reports which come from the northernmost station of Canada down into the main operational airports are centralized in this one area through this facsimile system and it is possible in a matter of seconds to obtain the weather conditions from one end of the country to another. For example, when I assisted at the inauguration of this facsimile system at

Dorval, together with the chief of air staff, I think it was possible in less than a second to obtain reports from Winnipeg and Gander on the condition of the weather over this facsimile instrument. Of course, the cost of that is somewhat high, as my hon. friend will appreciate.
There is an increase in office stationery, supplies and equipment of $84,000 and that is attributable as well in part to the facsimile system because it is necessary to have a special kind of paper not only in the Dorval area but at all of these airports in Canada.
Repairs and upkeep of buildings and works show an increase of $21,000 but that, I think, can be explained by the increase in other votes in similar subdivisions due to the increase in the cost of material and the like.

Item agreed to.

495. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, including construction work on municipal airports, $10,737,291.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to direct the minister's attention to the airport at Crumlin, Ontario, which serves London and the great majority of the western Ontario counties. In November, in the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I raised the question in this house and pointed out that this airport at Crumlin was the only airport which could be considered to be a major one between Toronto and Windsor. I also pointed out that it served one of our largest commercial and producing areas, concentrated in a comparatively small area in Canada. Perhaps at this stage I might ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong because the details are exclusively in the knowledge of the government, and of many of them I have no knowledge. However, at that time it was my understanding that an appropriation was to be made for the extension of the runways at the airport at Crumlin on the basis-
Perhaps my hon. friend will excuse me, but I do not quite understand him. Is he now referring to the London airport?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, but we call it the Crumlin airport because it is actually located at Crumlin. At that time it was my understanding the government were giving consideration to the spending of certain sums of money for the development of this airport into one which could take the largest and fastest types of aircraft now being used.
When the estimates appeared I was therefore somewhat surprised to find that no provision had been made for the extension of the 83276-384J
Supply-Transport
runways to permit either military aircraft or the larger and faster types of civilian aircraft to use this field, and it is a matter of very great concern within the city of London, not only so far as the municipal council is concerned, but particularly as regards the chamber of commerce.
The problem has recently been accentuated by the rumours which have appeared to the effect that consideration is being given to equipping No. 420 squadron of the Royal Canadian Air Force with a jet-type aircraft. If such is the case, and once again I would ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong, it would appear that jet-type aircraft cannot land or use the present facilities at the city of London airport. I might point out that No. 420 squadron of the air force is a most active squadron, training large numbers of personnel from London and district. In addition to that fact, there is located at this airfield or immediately adjacent to it one of the basic training centres operated by the air force for the training of NATO air personnel.
Once again I delve into the realm of conjecture. I am led to believe that certain overtures were made either by the department to the municipal authorities or the other way around, with respect to the future operation of this airfield. I am rising purely for the purpose of asking the minister to explain to us what has occurred, why there has been a diminution of interest, if such is the case, in the development of the city of London airport, and what the plans for the future are in so far as either military or civilian use of the airport is concerned.	,

I thank my hon. friend for his constructive intervention with reference to the London airport. Let me tell him that there is not the slightest indication on the part of officials of the department of lack of interest in that establishment. London has a very good airport-I have been there on at least two occasions-and it has many potentialities. Unfortunately, however, it is not one of the main major airports in Canada, and I do not say this in a derogatory sense at all. There are so many major airports in Canada that consideration has to be given to those first and foremost. It is a fact that in our first draft of estimates there was an item for the construction of a runway at London. But after consideration by treasury board, because of the demands that came from major airports and because of the over-all picture, it was decided not to pursue the matter and not to include it in the present estimates.
Then there was another feature which my hon. friend has raised, namely that having

Supply-Transport
to do with the R.C.A.F. It may very well be that the R.C.A.F. will require additional facilities at London. I am not competent to say whether that is so or not. But if additional facilities are required-and that was another matter that influenced treasury board in its decision-then national defence will ask us to build a runway. They will provide the funds and we will do it. That is generally the method by which we proceed. The decision is as I have stated it. It may be true that from a civilian standpoint it will be possible to include at a future date a sufficient sum of money to build a runway. However, I am frank with my hon. friend. I tell him what the decision is and I am afraid I cannot go any further,

Mr. Chairman, may I pursue this matter just one step further and ask the minister what was the outline of the negotiations, if any, which took place between the department and the city with respect to the taking over of the airport by the city? If there were any such negotiations, did that fact have any bearing on the subsequent disappearance from the estimates of any item for the extension of airport runways?

The only information I have is that to the authorities of the city we sent an officer who had some talks, but we have not had any information arising out of the visit of the Department of Transport official to the municipality.

Surveys have been made around Peterborough by the minister's department. Can the minister say what has been done with regard to the airport there? At present we have one which can take small planes. I just wondered whether the department was going to do something more for us.

Not at the moment, I am sorry to say. I am familiar with the situation because I have had several representations by both civic and other groups from Peterborough. In fairness to my hon. friend I may say that I believe he has also brought the matter to my attention. The point is that there are sites which might be adaptable for airport development. The decision of the department has been that in the case of a municipality, the municipality should make some contribution. At one time there was a question of assistance by way of groups other than municipal groups. While I have had representations to the effect that such contributions would be forthcoming, no firm offer has been made. To sum up the matter I would say this. There is the possibility of

development of airport sites in the Peterborough area. There would have to be representations either by the municipalities or by other groups. There have been some. However, there would have to be more firm representation before we would be in a position to say to what extent we could contribute to that project.
I thank the minister.

I should like to ask the
minister the position in connection with the Charlottetown airport. A year or two ago, I believe, there were negotiations between the minister's department and the city of Charlottetown with respect to extending the runways there and improving the airport generally. The minister is familiar with the amount of traffic that is borne from that airport and also with its inadequacy, especially from the point of view of the length of runways.
Then I had a more general question. Perhaps the minister could take it at the same time. I would appreciate it if he would bring us up to date on the position with regard to the Charlottetown airport and also if he would be kind enough to give the committee some information on the general revenue which is derived from some of the larger airports in Canada, from rentals or any other income from air lines and other users of the large airports. I should like to have an idea of what return there is on the investment, so to speak.

I shall be glad to review the position of the Charlottetown airport. My hon. friend will remember that when I was down to Charlottetown last year and met the mayor of the city together with one of the ministers of the Prince Edward Island government and some of the members of the legislature, my hon. friend was good enough to meet me at the hotel later on. The discussion centred around the policy of the government having to do with municipal assistance to airports. We viewed the location and agreed that it would be in the interests of aviation to extend the runway. There were two alternatives, but there was one alternative that our officers favoured; and I think on consideration the mayor and those interested on the island felt that it was the better of the two sites.
I outlined the policy. I indicated to the municipal authorities that the land would have to be expropriated by the municipalities and that we would provide the facilities. There has been some correspondence between the mayor and me-I now have to draw on my memory-the last of which outlined our

policy which is similar with reference to all municipalities. There has been no definite answer saying that the municipality would expropriate the land in question.
Although it has not come to me formally, there has been some suggestion that because this airport is on a trans-Canada route we should undertake to handle the whole expenditure which, in this case, would be quite considerable. That suggestion has not come to me formally and until it does I am not in a position to make any comment.
With reference to the second question my hon. friend asked, possibly I can pick out a number of the main airports. For instance, at Gander the revenue is $2,787,000, but I am sorry to say the expenditure is much higher than that. At Winnipeg the revenue is $137,000 and the expenditure is $74,000. At Toronto the revenue is $335,000 and the expenditure is $277,000. I think I should say in fairness to Gander that the position there is not comparable at the moment with the other airports, but I think in time the expenditure will be much lower than the revenue. At Dorval they break about even, with revenue being $765,000 compared with an expenditure of $800,000.

May I direct one or two further questions to the minister to clarify the position with respect to the London airport. First, what is the annual operating loss of the airport? Second, may I point out to him and ask for his comment on the fact that the city of London industrially is growing east. It must grow in that direction. With reference to the first question, the answer is that the annual operating loss was $60,000. As to the second question, I am sure my hon. friend would not expect me to be able to deal with the details of airport development. There are some 200 airports in Canada, and while I indicated earlier I had been at London on two occasions it is some time ago. I know that it is a fast growing industrial centre, and because of what I have seen at both Toronto and Montreal with respect to the rapidity of industrial development in the last few years in the vicinity of Malton and

Supply-Transport
Dorval I would not attempt to prognosticate anything so far as development at London is concerned. All I can say is that we have London very much in mind. However, I hope my hon. friend will realize that we have got to give attention to the major transcontinental airports. I know that T.C.A. is particularly interested in London. Why not include Peterborough?

Would the minister tell the committee what has happened with respect to the administration building at the airport at Saskatoon which, as he knows, is in the constituency of Rosthern.

When I was there recently pretty fair progress had been made. As the hon. member for Rosthern knows, the contract was awarded to an excellent contractor and it is expected that the terminal building will be ready for operation this fall.

I wonder whether the minister can make a statement as to what progress is being made towards the establishment of more adequate civilian facilities at the Comox airport? Is he in a position to make a statement at this time?

I am informed that is a military station. That matter is now under discussion with the air force which has it in hand, but just what it is proposed to do I do not know. It is not a civilian airport. My officer informs me that facilities will be installed some time this year by the Department of National Defence.
Do I understand that when an airport is built on a main line of T.C.A. the entire expenditure is paid by the department?

I could not answer affirmatively in a broad way. It depends on the circumstances in each case. Some airports right on the transcontinental route are owned by the municipalities. The municipalities make a substantial contribution toward them, but most of the expenditures are made by the Department of Transport for runways,
'Mr. Chevrier.]
lighting facilities, meteorological service and the like. The contribution of the municipality, as a rule, is their retention of the land and then the operation of the airport itself. What is done from time to time is a contribution to a municipality in an isolated area. I would not take it that my hon. friend's constituency is in that category, but it is, I know, in one of the important parts of Ontario.
As my hon friend knows, we have in the past used the United States field on the T.C.A. run. There is no assurance that will always be the case.

Air transport board-
501.	Salaries and other expenses, including the Canadian delegation to the international civil aviation organization, $274,089.

I take it that one of the main objectives of the air transport board is to promote civil aviation in Canada. It would seem that the main function of this governmental body is to carry on work of that kind. Would the minister explain why there is not a more determined effort to give government flying work to the flying companies. Apparently quite a lot of government flying is done by the R.C.A.F. It does seem to me that some of this could be turned over to the civilian companies.
For example, I got a return earlier in the session which showed that the R.C.A.F. had carried for the Iron Ore Company of Canada, which as the minister knows is the company developing the northern Quebec and Labrador iron ore deposits, 989,432 pounds of cargo and 121 passengers, and had done 181-15 hours of flying, for which they were paid. My information is that there were civilian companies in a position to do that flying. Apparently the Iron Ore Company came to the government with a story that there was great need for fast action. They may have felt that the civilian companies would charge a little more than the R.C.A.F., but it does seem to me there should be an explanation as to why private work of that kind is taken away from a private flying company.
Surely, we are not financing the air force to do work of that kind. This seems to me to be one way of fostering the development of civil aviation in Canada, which after all is the basis of the whole industry. I was not in the east at the time, but I understand there were press reports to the effect that one member of the air transport board had objected, and had taken the position that this work should have been done by a private company rather than by the R.C.A.F. It would appear that he was correct.
There is other work being done, such as flying into these meteorological stations which come under the Minister of Transport. I understand that is being done by the R.C.A.F. Why should it not be possible for flying of that type to be done by the private companies? Then, again, there are the ice patrols on the Atlantic coast, and that work is done by the R.C.A.F. I see no reason why it could
Supply-Transport
not be done by the private companies. The United States has a different policy. There they give every encouragement to the private firms, and I believe in the continental United States they even have a lot of defence force flying done by the civilian companies.
The minister's department is the one that should be looking after the promotion of civilian flying. The defence department can look after the air force. I do not understand why more aggressive steps are not taken by the Department of Transport to see that flying of the type I have mentioned is done by private Canadian companies.

My hon. friend is quite right in his assumption that the civil aviation division of the Department of Transport should give every encouragement to civilian flying. I can assure him that we do. I wish my hon. friend knew what co-operation and co-ordination there is between the air transport board and officers of the Department of Transport and groups of civilian flying organizations, flying clubs, IATA, ICAO, and the many other groups. It is the object of the officials in the department to make sure that civilian flying is given every opportunity.
We do see to it that government work is given to civilian companies. In fact we have a directive that goes to every department of government indicating to all those departments using flying services that they must ask civilians for service. That directive has had the approval of my colleagues in the government. Further than that, officials in the other departments see to it that that directive is put into effect.
Now, that is not the case in connection with the R.C.A.F. or defence work. It is not possible for this department to control the activities of the Department of National Defence.
My hon. friend has asked about flying in connection with the meteorological stations in the north. Those stations that are concerned with the Department of National Defence are handled by that department; and I do not think my hon. friend would expect it to be otherwise. After all, these are joint operational weather stations under the plan between Canada and the United States, and they are pretty close to being on the secret list. It is felt that they should be serviced by the R.C.A.F.; and they have been. I think there is a valid reason for it.

In fact this year it was Maritime Central that had it; and I believe Northern Wings may have had it on a previous occasion.

Well, he would get clearance through the air transport board only if it was clear that there were no civilian air lines able to do it. perhaps a great portion of it- was strategic. That may have prompted the decision that was taken in this instance.
