speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in support of representations that have already been made at this session with respect to the need for a greater number of grade crossing separations in this country. Other hon. members have given statistics and examples as to the loss of life that takes place because of accidents between trains and automobiles. It does seem to me that it may be necessary to revise the formula or to change the policy so that a large number of grade crossings at which accidents are taking place might be eliminated as level crossings.
I buttress what I am trying to say in connection with this matter by drawing attention to one particular level crossing to which I have referred in the house on a number of occasions. I refer to the point where the heavily travelled thoroughfare between the city of Winnipeg and the town of Transcona crosses the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That crossing is actually within the city limits of Winnipeg but, as I pointed out, it is a main thoroughfare between those two communities. On one previous occasion, after I had raised this question a number of times, the minister pointed out to me that the crossing in question is protected by gates that come down halfway across the thoroughfare, and also by a signal system which operates as well as such a system can operate. It is my contention that that is really not good enough. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press of August 15, 1953, which reports a tragic accident which took place on August 14, at that crossing. I say it was a tragedy. A gentleman who lived in Transcona died as a result of the accident. What I wish to point out is that this accident shows up the inadequacy of those halfway gates, signals, bells, lights and what-have-you.
Supply-Transport
According to the report in the Winnipeg Free Press, this man was driving from Transcona to Winnipeg and stopped at the crossing because there was a train travelling east. He waited of course until the train went by, but just as the train went over the crossing he started his truck to move west on into Winnipeg. The noise of the train travelling east made it impossible for him to hear another train that was coming west at the same time. He thought the road was clear, but what happened was that he drove right into the path of this oncoming westbound train. The newspaper report indicates that the man lost his life and that the truck was demolished.
I simply cite that instance, along with others that other hon. members have been speaking about during the discussion of the minister's estimates, to point out the inadequacy of signal lights, bells and even gates. What is needed at crossings such as this, where there is heavy traffic, is a grade separation. I point out that it is a very busy spot, where the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway east and west crosses the heavily travelled thoroughfare between Winnipeg and Transcona.
I know that one of the other answers the minister has given on previous occasions is that this case and others like it should go before the board of transport commissioners, and that whether or not a separation could be made depends upon whether the municipalities and the railway concerned are prepared to put up the necessary money. That being the case, it seems to me that some revising of that formula, some revising of government policy in connection with this matter, is indicated. What happened here happens far too often across the country. Because of our responsibility for protecting life and limb in this country, I hope that something will be done to revise that policy so that more of these grade crossings can be eliminated.

May I say I think the hon. member and the committee will get a great deal of satisfaction from the report on the grade crossing investigation which I shall table before the end of the session. It is a lengthy report, and it makes a number of recommendations, all of which I think are to the good, recommendations regarding an amendment to the Railway Act. It would be well if the committee and the government as well had an opportunity of studying the document before the next session, because it has come down too late in this session to take any action on it. I hope, now that I have given that assurance, the committee will
6080

Supply-Transport
not enter into a discussion on individual grade crossings, because quite a number of them have been discussed earlier.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that he is going to table a copy of that report at this session?

Yes, and it will contain some very vital recommendations, many of which -I will go further and say I hope most of which-we shall be able to implement by way of legislation; but I cannot at this stage be prognosticating government policy. Since I have said that, I would hope that hon. members would be reasonable in their discussion of this because, if my recollection serves me right, there are 33,000 level crossings in Canada, and I know there are many in each constituency, and we could go on at some length discussing them. I would not say this if I were not going to table the report, which I assure the committee is an excellent document.

What precautions will be taken when new railway lines are built, such as those proposed to be built in the near future, to prevent the building of level crossings that at a later date will have to be eliminated at a great expense?

Most of the railways that are being built and have been built in the last several years are built in the wilderness, so that the question does not arise and will not arise until the population in those areas increases far more than it is now.

What I mean to say is that provision should be made so that that does not occur. Perhaps liaison with the provincial departments of highways and municipalities could be brought about so that proper provision might be made for at least some of the railway crossings that cross main highways.

I am afraid the minister is forever going to associate me with the Credit-ville crossing. I have mentioned this level crossing on various occasions in the house and I have had some correspondence with the minister on it, which he has always received sympathetically. An hon. member to my left thanked the minister earlier this afternoon for airports and assistance to some other ports in the country. I hope that this time next year I shall be in a position to do the same with respect to this Creditville crossing which is located seven miles east of Woodstock.
In view of the remarks the minister has just made, I do not intend to make any extensive remarks, but I know that there are many level crossings in Canada. I think this is

probably one of the worst, and from an economic point of view would be one of the most easily eliminated. Since I have sent the minister a copy of this, for the purpose of the record I would like to read briefly from the London Free Press of Friday, June 11, at page 10:
The C.N.R. crossing on No. 2 highway near Creditville, commonly called, "suicide crossing" has been the scene of 24 accidents resulting in one fatality, 10 injured and damage estimated at $8,425 in a little over a year.
The article goes on to cite some further information. I might say that these statistics are not quite up to date, because since June 8 there have been two additional deaths and several injured at this crossing. That damage figure of $8,425 does not include the damages awarded in extensive and expensive litigation. I have already mentioned it several times, and I hope the minister will consider it with some sympathy.
In the neighbouring city of Stratford someone wrote a book called "Renown at Stratford". I hope someone will write a book about this crossing and call it "Carnage at Creditville".

I hope in the recommendations which have been made there is a suggestion that the freight cars be painted along the bottom of the side so that there will not be so many of these crossing accidents in which the automobiles crash into a stationary train, especially on a rainy night. That is how a great number of these accidents take place.
I do not wish to anticipate what is in the report.
I thought you knew what was in it.
I know what the recommendations are but I think perhaps they should be made public when the report is tabled.

Would the minister comment on the possibility of providing in the case of individual railway construction that where the main line of a railway meets a highway there shall be from there on either an underpass or an overpass. Would it not be possible to provide for that in the bill covering railway construction?

There is a discussion of that very point in the report which will be tabled although I am not quite sure whether there is a recommendation. However, since there has been a discussion on the point I hope my hon. friend will be prepared to allow the matter to stand meantime.

Perhaps the minister, before he leaves for the St. Lawrence seaway development project, might leave this indelible mark on the transport legislation of Canada. In fact, it might well be his valedictory to introduce legislation to that effect. That would seem to be most appropriate because otherwise we are going to go on having these jurisdictional conflicts between the province and the dominion as to whose responsibility it is to provide for crossings or underpasses. Surely it could be clearly provided-the minister should not get annoyed because we wish him well in his new appointment.
My hon. friend is getting annoyed. I am not getting annoyed.
Well, the minister looks cross.
How could I look cross at my hon. friend?

I am glad to hear the minister say that. I would like to see him do something about this because this is the last opportunity we will have to discuss this proposition with the minister, who has held his present position for ten years or so and is thoroughly familiar with the problem, more so than anyone else will be for a number of years. He is well aware of the difficulties which surround this question of final responsibility, and whether it is the responsibility of the province to put a road under the railway or the responsibility of the railway to put a road over the highway. Surely it is about time some legislation were enacted which would lay this down clearly with respect to future railway construction. It seems to me to be reasonable that in the case of a main line it should be clearly designated that such a line will be the joint responsibility of the railway and the province with respect to providing a grade crossing over that line.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure no one knows better than my hon. friend the great difficulties surrounding this problem and the government was made fully aware of them after it received certain representations from the board of transport commissioners. That is why we asked the board to study the whole railway-highway crossing problem and matters relating thereto. The board have studied this question and my answer to my hon. friend is to let us see what the board recommends in the report which will be tabled before the end of the session. I have obtained permission from my colleagues in the government to give the house the assurance that it will be tabled. But it must be printed in English and in French and there are quite a number of 83276-3854
Supply-Transport
copies to be made. It is not yet ready but I hope it will be on, shall I say, Friday, and if not then early next week. If perchance the house were to adjourn or prorogue before the report is tabled I will see to it that each member of the house gets a copy of the report.
I hope the minister will insist on its being tabled in time so that he may introduce some recommendations with respect thereto, because I can think of no more lasting memorial-

Is this the time for
obituaries?

-than legislation dealing with this difficult and vexing question which is of interest not only to his own province but to every province of Canada and to those of us who have to travel the highway and cross railway tracks. Without making any commitment I might say that I would be glad to receive the minister's report and his recommendations; for in view of his long experience I think his recommendations would be quite sound.

Item agreed to.
Canadian maritime commission-[DOT]
503.	Administration, $160,520.

When will the annual report of the Canadian maritime commission be available? That report covers the year to March 31 and under the act the government has only three months in which to table it. Will we be able to get it before the house prorogues?
I am informed it will be ready for tabling before the end of the session.
Can the minister tell the committee whether all of the Canadian deep-sea cargo vessels for which approval for transfer to the United Kingdom registry was sought have now been transferred?

All the applications that have been made to the maritime commission have been approved by the commission for furtherance to the British ministry of transport, and all except two have been approved by the British ministry of transport.

When all those ships have been transferred to the United Kingdom registry what will be the number of deep-sea cargo vessels on the Canadian registry? I dealt with this on May 13 as reported at page 4706 of Hansard and my information at that time was that by the time all these transfers had gone through there would only remain 21 dry cargo deep-sea vessels in Canada's merchant fleet. I would like to have the minister

Supply-Transport
verify these figures. I will give him the list. Once these transfers have gone through the total number of deep-sea dry cargo vessels, which, of course, would not include the tankers, would be 21, and of that number 7 would be engaged in coastal trade and not in deep-sea service. Another 8 would comprise the Canadian National Steamships fleet, and I understand there would be only two of the wartime 10,000-tonners left in deep-sea service, one 4,000-tonner built in wartime, and 3 other vessels, none of which would be modern ships. Can the minister tell me whether or not those figures are accurate? If not, can he give me accurate figures in those categories.

As far as I can ascertain, the hon. gentleman's figure is as accurate as we can have it at this moment, namely, that there are 21 dry-cargo vessels but all of them are deep-sea and none of them are coastal.

I said "are engaged in the coastal trade". I am informed that seven out Of the 21 are not engaged in the deep-sea trade but are engaged in the coastal trade. That would leave only 14 Canadian vessels in the deep-sea trade.
The information I have is that four are engaged in the coastal trade and that the others are engaged in ocean trade.
How many of the 10,000-tonners built during the war are engaged in the deep-sea trade? The figure I gave the minister was two.
It is difficult to give a firm answer because of the position of the transfers and the applications that have been made.
I mean where the transfers have gone through.
Assuming that they have gone through, there will be about three or four 10,000-tonners engaged in the deep-sea trade and three in the coastal trade.

How many of the 4,000-
tonners?
One in the coastal trade and eight in the deep sea trade.
Will those eight all be Canadian National Steamships vessels?
I think they will be.
Is it a fact that the Canadian deep-sea fleet will be the smallest that it has been in 35 years?

I am not able to say. I would have to go back to the figures I had on the

original debate. In the post-war periods I think it has been at a low level compared with war periods. But having regard to other countries, the comparison is good. When one considers that we will be able to call on the ships that have been transferred-some 91 ships or more to the United Kingdom-under the NATO plan whereby ships are to be pooled, and having regard to the circumstances in this peacetime situation in which we find ourselves, I cannot say that the position is detrimental.

That is a statement which hardly reflects the actual condition, I am afraid. However, have any of these ships which have been transferred to the United Kingdom registry been modernized or is there any arrangement or plan under way for changing those vessels to modern cargo vessels?
I am informed that there is a new cargo vessel now building in the United Kingdom for a Canadian owner and that two others are in contemplation. These will add three ships to the merchant fleet.

Will they be under United
Kingdom registry?

They will be under the
Canadian flag.
Are they replacing ships which have been transferred to United Kingdom registry or are they new ships for Canada?
They are new ships.
No attempt whatsoever is being made to convert the ships which have gone to United Kingdom registry into modern cargo vessels?

There have been some
applications. There is one application that I can think of that is under consideration but it has not been dealt with definitely yet.

Has the government made any change whatever in its policy with regard to the merchant marine since the statement of the minister on November 12 last year? At that time he set out the policy. Under that policy as announced there has been no improvement in the situation of which I am aware. From the minister's answers today it is perfectly obvious that the Canadian deep-sea cargo fleet has been liquidated. As he says, we have three or perhaps four old, 10,000-ton wartime freighters. So far the result of this policy has been nil having regard to Canada's procuring a modern deep-sea fleet. I think that is one of the greatest tragedies in the post-war period. The minister tries to compare our position with that

of other nations. But the fact is that Switzerland is going to have a much greater merchant navy than Canada. That fact just shows how ridiculous the situation is. Is the government making any change in the plan, or is the same old situation to exist?
I would rather put it this way: There has been no change since the later of the two statements.
What was that?

Since the later of the two statements I made in the House of Commons. My hon. friend asks if there has been any change since my statement in November. I made another statement. My hon. friend has made several speeches to which I have had to reply, the latest of which was on the first item of these estimates. I can say this. There has been no change since that time, and the position remains as it was when I made that intervention. I think it would be some three weeks ago; it might be a little bit less or it might be a little bit more. I then gave the reasons for the decision. I hope my hon. friend will not invite me to go into the whole policy again. It has been put on record twice. I have given him frank answers to the questions he put. There is no change in the policy. That is all I can say other than this, as I emphasized the last time I spoke: The matter is still under review. I cannot repeat now why it has been impossible to subsidize ships either from a capital standpoint or from an operational standpoint. However the position today is substantially what it was about three weeks ago.

I have one other question. How would the minister propose to man any of these ships that were brought back from United Kingdom registry, now that the Canadian seamen have been dispersed to other jobs all over the country?
We have a million tons of other shipping-coastal and inland lakes shipping-that gives us the nucleus from which to get men.

I do not want to prolong the discussion any further, Mr. Chairman. The minister knows exactly where we stand on this question. I hope the cabinet will give further consideration to this problem once the house has prorogued. By the time we come back next fall or after the new year I hope there will have been adopted or worked out a policy which will bring about the objective placed before the government by its own maritime commission several years ago, namely, that Canada would have
Supply-Transport
a deep-sea merchant fleet containing a nucleus of modern, fast, cargo vessels. I am afraid it is too late. I am afraid that the die has been cast and the situation cannot be remedied. Perhaps the minister is right that consideration even at this late date would prevent this tragedy occurring, and I do hope he will give the whole question further consideration.
Have we any oil tankers sailing under the Canadian flag other than those of the Royal Canadian Navy?
Yes, we have eleven.
I think this is the appropriate item for me to ask this question. As the minister knows, since the C.P.R. discontinued the steamer service on the Arrow lakes-
That comes under the next item, the subvention item.
Oh, I am very hopeful.

Item agreed to.
504.	Steamship subventions for coastal services, as detailed in the estimates, $4,147,725.

As the minister knows, since the Canadian Pacific Railway Company discontinued the steamer service on the Arrow lakes the residents of the upper Arrow lakes have been without any form of commercial water transport and have suffered great inconvenience. However the flame of hope has been kept alive in their breasts owing to periodic announcements by the minister of public works of British Columbia and certain press statements that negotiations are proceeding with the minister's department or the maritime commission with respect to a subsidy or a joint subsidy. Can the minister inform the house what has happened in connection with that application?

Yes. I have been in communication with the minister of public works of the province of British Columbia who is arranging for an application for a subsidy on the Arrow lakes. The matter is now before the maritime commission for study.
Thank you.

I regret to say that owing to the decision of the house with respect to the last redistribution bill the area about which the hon. member for Kootenay West speaks is no longer in my constituency, but I should like to say a word. There is, I think, no more romantic or scenic area in the whole Dominion of Canada than the Arrow lakes.
Come down to Bonavista.

Bring your sou'wester.

Supply-Transport
So speaks the old salt.

Of course I am sure that the area represented by the minister who has just spoken is scenic, but unfortunately it is fogbound for one half of the year and icebound for the other half, which seems to me to have dictated the state of mind of the Secretary of State.
There is more than one kind of fog.

I was speaking of an area of Canada which is neither fogbound nor icebound. I am not going to keep the committee for long, but I want to say that in the first place I cannot understand the apparent lack of interest taken in this area by the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is one of the pioneer districts in the province of British Columbia, particularly in the interior, and I cannot help but think that if the Canadian Pacific Railway had been a little more aggressive in their requests to the federal government we might have had a subsidy for the continuation of the steamer service on the Arrow lakes. Whatever the decision may be on the merits of the application, it is one of the most scenic tourist areas of the whole province and of the whole dominion. It is not only one of the most scenic areas, it is one of the oldest routes of communication between the prairie provinces and the Pacific coast.
Since 1811.

As the hon. member for Kootenay West points out, since 1811. Whether it is because of lack of interest on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway or lack of understanding on the part of the federal Department of Transport I do not know. I do not care to assess the responsibility, but it seems to me that it is the greatest pity-
In view of what my hon. friend said a moment ago, surely it cannot be lack of interest in the Department of Transport.
Then what the minister is indicating is that the Canadian Pacific Railway has not pursued actively enough its request for a subsidy.
I was not indicating that at all.

Then I wish the minister would indicate exactly what he does mean. As I say, I am not prepared to assess the responsibility. I speak only from the point of view of one from the interior of the province of

British Columbia. Shortly there is to be a conducted tour, if I may call it that, of members of parliament and their wives to the province of British Columbia, and I regret exceedingly that they are not going to go down from Revelstoke through the Arrow lakes to the constituency of the hon. member for Kootenay West and from there back up through the Okanagan to Kamloops and on down to Vancouver.
I simply want to support the request made by the hon. member for Kootenay West for consideration by the federal Department of Transport of an adequate subsidy to enable the company to continue its service on the Arrow lakes which has been one of the pioneer routes through British Columbia and has been in continuous operation since 1898. From the point of view of both tourist and commercial activities, it would be a great pity if the service were to be permanently discontinued.

Can the minister tell the committee what success has been achieved in the discussions respecting the reducing of congestion on the subsidized route between Wood Island, Prince Edward Island, and Caribou, Nova Scotia. I realize that a new boat is being built, but I am thinking of the immediate problem for this summer and next summer until the new boat is put into service.

There have been a number of discussions between officials of the company, Northumberland Ferries, the government of Prince Edward Island and the maritime commission. A number of suggestions have been made to meet the increased traffic during the course of the present season. One of the first suggestions made was a very excellent one which the commission was prepared to accept but on proceeding further it was found that some of the conditions could not be met by the applicant. I hesitate to go into the details because they concern a private financial undertaking on the part of Northumberland Ferries. However, I believe the matter is being given additional study by the commission now.

Can the minister state what company receives the subvention and provides the service between Pictou, Charlottetown and the Magdalen islands which is listed in the details, and what is the frequency of the service?

It is with fear and trembling that I ask what is the reason for the reduction of $100,000 under western local services. Surely that would have nothing to do with the service on the west coast of Vancouver island, would it?
The reduction concerns the Canadian Pacific Steamships subsidy and was brought about because the ship was withdrawn.

Yes, but if a subsidy were provided might they not be able to find another ship? The situation on the west coast of Vancouver island is serious. There are many places you cannot reach by road. These people have been there for nearly a century now and they have had to depend entirely on the steamship service. For instance, I have in my constituency quite a flourishing fishing and logging village, Port Renfrew. The people there are dependent upon their mail and all their freight coming in by the steamship service. Unless they are able to use the facilities of the private logging companies they are dependent upon the steamship service going up the west coast.
This is a very serious situation for these people who have been in here for many, many years. There is an area which, potentially, could be of tremendous economic value. Not only are there the logging camps, the fishing camps, but there is also a considerable amount of mining farther up the west coast of Vancouver island.
Is it not possible to provide some form of assistance which would make it possible for some other company to operate the service if the Canadian Pacific has not a vessel now? I know the vessel they had was worn out and was not considered safe for the exposed passage, because you get the full sweep of the Pacific ocean up against those shores. You cannot put on any little lake steamer. There are these thriving communities all up the coast of Vancouver island, and I wonder what these people are going to do.

I do not know whether my hon. friend understood me or if I did not make my position clear. This $100,000 subsidy was not turned down. I hope there is no misunderstanding as to that. If some other company will make an application for service, I am sure the maritime commission will be glad to give it consideration. Since the withdrawal of the particular ship and the contract which operated between the maritime commission and the Canadian Pacific there has been no further application. I can suggest this to my hon. friend. If the
Supply-Transport
Canadian Pacific will make application for another ship or some other company interested in the area would make application,
I am sure the commission would be glad to consider it.
Thank you very much; the door is not closed to another company?
Certainly not.

I want to ask a question concerning the Wood Island-Caribou service. Following the breakdown of negotiations between the company and the maritime commission, I understand that the commission was looking into the possibility of buying the Lady Alexandra on the west coast, so that additional service could be put into operation this year. I am wondering if that has been abandoned or whether that is still a possibility?

I am sorry that I cannot add to what I have already indicated, namely, that we have been in communication and negotiation with both the Northumberland Ferries Limited and the members of the Prince Edward Island government in connection with additional facilities and in connection with the operation of the new ship. Those negotiations are still continuing.
I take it that that would mean there is still some possibility of extra service being provided before the new boat is completed?

I hope so, but I am not in
a position to say so now because I do not know where the negotiations stand.

Item agreed to.
National harbours board-*
505. Advances to national harbours board, subject to the provisions of section 29 of the National Harbours Board Act, to meet expenditures applicable to the calendar year 1954 on any or all of the following accounts:
Reconstruction and capital expenditures-Halifax, $989,500; Saint John, $1,815,000; Quebec, $1,365,000; Churchill, $900,000; generally unforeseen and miscellaneous, $200,000; total, $5,269,500.
Less-Amount to be expended from replacement funds, $387,000; $4,882,500.

This is the first item for the national harbours board, and I wish the minister would explain to the committee what course is followed by this board when it gives consideration to the necessity for new buildings in the harbours. For example, this spring we have had the position stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that because Vancouver harbour is unable to handle any more wheat the price of wheat at Fort William had to be cut lower than the price at Vancouver. Of course, this is a sore point

Supply-Transport
on the west coast, and we will deal with it under the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Has the national harbours board given any consideration to the need for further elevator accommodation at the port of Vancouver? Surely it is their responsibility to see that the facilities in these ports are adequate to meet conditions from time to time. However, we have a statement from one of the ministers, and a senior minister, with regard to the capacity of Vancouver harbour to handle wheat.
It appears to me that there should be steps taken to increase the capacity at the port. We do not want to get into a position where wheat that should go through the west coast is being diverted through Fort William and Port Arthur, simply because Vancouver does not have adequate accommodation. I should like to have the minister's comment on that situation. Then there is another point I want to raise in connection with Vancouver harbour.

With respect to the general policy of the board, the board has been giving consideration to the acute situation in the elevators under its jurisdiction for the past two years, and I would say quite actively during the last year. It has, because of the position it found in Montreal, Halifax, and Churchill, been able to recommend extensions there.
In Vancouver my hon. friend will remember the national harbours board were in a very embarrassing position at one time, and that not so long ago, when there were two leased elevators on which the leases expired and which the lessee did not see fit to renew. The national harbours board had to advertise, and it was some time before they could get someone to renew this lease. The position was so bad that they even had to advertise in the United States, with the result they succeeded in getting United States interests to take over both the elevators in question. I am informed by the board that there has been delivered and moved out of Vancouver more wheat this year than ever before. In fact I think the record will indicate there has been twice as much,
No, the minister had better check that. The last word I had was that it did not even equal last year.

I am informed that compared with the corresponding period last year there has been twice as much wheat moved through the elevators at Vancouver; that is the information I have.
Now, with regard to the additional facilities, they are under constant review. If the

national harbours board, which is a government agency and not a departmental agency, wants to make recommendations for additional facilities and extensions, they will be considered in the same manner as extensions at other places.

In the vote there is $989,500 for capital expenditures at Halifax, and an additional $550,000 in the supplementaries; $1,815,000 for Saint John and an additional $350,000 in the supplementary estimates; $1,365,000 for Quebec and $900,000 for Churchill as well as $200,000 for unforeseen expenditures. This situation is serious. The government itself said that the port is operating practically to capacity, so far as the shipment of wheat is concerned. I cannot understand why the national harbours board has not taken some steps to meet that situation. We are the port farthest removed from Ottawa and, incidentally, the port through which pass by far the greatest number of ships. There is no reason why the national harbours board should not be right up to the minute on this situation. It is not good enough to say that because two or three years ago they had to lease an elevator to an American company there is no need today for further elevator space.
I do not begrudge expenditures appearing in the estimates in connection with other ports. However I would ask the government whether it has under consideration the possibility of extending the facilities at the port of Vancouver for the handling of wheat.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister replies may I say that this is an important point, provided that there is in Vancouver a demand for additional facilities. If those who administer the port at Vancouver have made a request for additional facilities I would like to know why there is no item in the estimates to provide them with those facilities. If they have not made a request then I take it they must feel that the facilities at the port of Vancouver which, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has said, is the busiest all-year-round port in Canada, are sufficient to provide for the traffic there.
I would not care to associate myself with a demand for further or greater expenditures of money at the port of Vancouver by the harbour commissioners there just because a considerable amount of money has been spent in other harbours across Canada. But if the harbour commissioners at Vancouver have indicated to the minister that there is a need for further facilities at that port to

take care of the traffic, then I would insist that Vancouver receive equal consideration with those other ports.

May I say in answer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway that I should like to confirm what I said earlier about the movement of wheat through Vancouver. Up to the end of May of this year it was 49,442,017 bushels as compared with 26,113,000 up to the end of May of last year.
But the record for a year is over 100,000,000 bushels.

So that is about twice as much, up to now. Then dealing with facilities: I am sure my hon. friend would not want to have additional facilities there if they were not required. I thought the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway put it pretty clearly. The national harbours board think there are sufficient facilities for grain handling at Vancouver. As a matter of fact there are facilities to move 18,716,000 bushels of grain.
Where?
At Vancouver.
In what period?

That is the capacity of the elevators, as compared with the 15 million bushels at Montreal. So the board feel that with the facilities now owned by private enterprise there is sufficient to meet the demand. If the time arrives when the facilities are not adequate we will build extensions to the present elevators.
Then I understand the board is making no recommendation whatever for any increase in grain handling facilities at Vancouver; is that right?
There has been no recommendation made to me for that purpose.

Has any consideration been given by the government to the setting up of advisory councils in any of these national harbours, for instance at Vancouver? I think there was a recommendation of that kind contained in the report of Sir Alexander Gibb back in the early thirties, when he investigated the situation in all the national ports in Canada. Here is a good example where there would be benefit from having some local council advising the national harbours board.
The present situation is that you have three commissioners sitting here in Ottawa, 2,500 miles away; and I do not believe there is any representative from the west coast on that
Supply-Transport
board. It would be far more beneficial to the port if there were some local committee able to advise. As I have said, Sir Alexander Gibb did make a recommendation along that line. I believe his suggestion was that there should be representatives of the city government, the shipping interests, labour unions and the like. Has any consideration been given by the government to a council of that kind at Vancouver?

The answer is no, because that is one of the recommendations of Sir Alexander Gibb that the government did not accept. There were many it did accept, but that is one it did not see fit to implement. There are many reasons, which I have put on the record from time to time, as to why the government did not feel it was advisable.
I can say that in the port of Halifax they felt rather strongly about that recommendation at one time. They have abandoned their plea for it, and have adopted a port club known as the port of Halifax club. I am told that it is properly known as the port of Halifax commission. That commission is composed of a group of local people who are interested in the port and who communicate with the national harbours board from time to time. As the hon. member knows, the national harbours board is a body which visits each of the harbours from time to time and meets these commissions. It meets a similar group in the city of Quebec. If other groups in Vancouver feel they would like to do the same thing, I am sure the national harbours board would meet them. But it was found inadvisable to accept the recommendation of the Gibb report.

I have one further question. Within the last few days a large quantity of crude oil has been pumped into Vancouver harbour through a mistake made by an employee of the Imperial Oil Limited, as a result of which 18 miles of the waterfront have been affected. A newspaper dispatch of June 11 states that-
-4,000 barrels of heavy oil spilled into the inlet from loco refinery May 28.
Now Imperial Oil is busy having it cleaned up. The dispatch continues:
Vancouver's biggest, most expensive spring cleaning job-removal of oil from Burrard inlet beaches -will cost thousands of dollars and will take weeks or months to complete.
What is the position of the national harbours board in a case of this kind? Have they had any report about this condition? This is the case of a company contaminating these beaches. Here is a case of a company contaminating those beaches and causing thousands of dollars worth of damage in

Supply-Transport

Mr. Chairman, with the permission of the hon. member for Kamloops, who ordinarily would speak first on these estimates, I should like to speak for a moment or two because unfortunately I have an appointment elsewhere which will take me out of the chamber in a very few moments. As this is the general item dealing with the administration of the Department of the Secretary of State, there is one matter that does not come directly within the estimates on which I should like to comment for a few moments. I refer to what in my opinion is the unfortunate situation now existing in so far as awards of recognition to Canadian civilian personnel are concerned. We have a situation in this country where those who have served the state-and I use "state" as a very general term-for many years, and whom one might think were entitled to some recognition, find that there is nothing in the gift of the government of Canada which can be given them by way of such recognition.
Some may remember that I raised this matter some time ago and gave the illustration of a lady who had worked on the piers in Halifax for a matter of some twenty or thirty years going back to the first war. She had served the soldiers going through the piers at that time with coffee, and continued on with immigrants during the twenties and thirties and into the forties. When she reached


certainly a rather advanced age the department suggested that she was too old to do this. She never received a cent of salary and they employed someone else to do the work. It was suggested that possibly some little award of recognition might be given her and I was told that no such thing was permitted. I do not think that is right.
We talk a great deal today, and properly so, of the development of the Canadian status. We take pride in the development of a Canadian nationalism. We hear talk about a Canadian flag and all these other things which go towards the national development of Canada. Yet we find that on a national basis we have no way by which we can give recognition to those who have served the state, using the word in a very general way. If one has achieved prominence in the academic world, the industrial world or the world of politics, universities will give recognition. We have sitting in this chamber those who have achieved awards of doctor's degrees, and they have been earned. Even in the churches there are titles which are conferred. I understand there is an order of knighthood in one of the great churches of this country.
There was a time when we did give awards, and I want to make it very plain that I am not now suggesting for a moment anything of a hereditary nature. We are not talking about peerages or anything of that kind. Any awards given will have to be won by the individual himself, must be worn by the individual and must die with the individual. I am not suggesting even an order of knighthood although personally-
Or even a crystal ball.

Or even a crystal ball, as my hon. friend says. I would not be averse to seeing the knighthood title "Sir" bestowed in certain cases. I remember that a former chief justice of Nova Scotia who died not long ago carried that title with dignity and respect and won the approbation not only of the bar but of the province as a whole. But I want to make it plain that I am not discussing anything of a hereditary nature or even the restoration of such orders, but I do say that I think the time has come when we should restore some of the orders that have been within the gift of the government before and which I find have now apparently been done away with.
I am quite sure the Secretary of State will say: Far be it from me to be vested with the responsibility of making recommendations in such a matter. I know it would not be easy to decide. Undoubtedly there would be newspapers which would say that these were political awards, that it was a terrible thing and that it should not be left to politicians

to make such recommendations. That may be a fair criticism but I would say that after all the antennae of politicians are fairly well tuned to the public current and public opinion, and I am quite sure that no recommendations would be made to the Secretary of State, whoever he might be, which did not meet with the approval of the people within the constituency concerned.
Personally, having played a little bit of politics for more years than I like to remember, the only thing I have ever got out of a federal government, Liberal or Conservative, is the satisfaction I got in the thirties of recommending a man who had given over forty years to the Boy Scout movement and who certainly made an impression on my life as he did on all the boys within that community. I suggested to a certain person that his name might be considered for the O.B.E. That recommendation was considered and ultimately he received the award. I know that it was one which certainly met with the approval not only of the people of the community but of the whole province.
It is something like that that I have in mind. As far as I know the great race to the south of us has no civilian awards whatsoever. I suppose that is part of their traditions. When they broke with the crown at the time of the American revolutionary war they resented any suggestion of preferment and apparently the tradition was established that no such awards would be given. But, without speaking at all critically, when one sees the number of Kentucky colonels, shall we say, created in that country from year to year and realizes that anyone who is elected to office, even that of justice of the peace, bears the title "honourable" for the rest of his life, I think he can say that even there there is a desire to have some recognition of some kind.
I have checked the situation in the commonwealth countries. We know of course that in Great Britain a multitude of titles and preferments can be created. I am not speaking now of the peerage or knighthood. There are some very select ones such as Companion of Honour, Order of Merit and others that are given to the individual, and there are also the orders of the British Empire, the C.B.E., O.B.E. and M.B.E. The same applies in Australia and New Zealand. In those countries they have a civilian list and a military list. In Canada we had a civilian list and a military list, and up until some time after 1935 civilian awards were made. Then they were discontinued.
During the last war many civilian awards of the British Empire were made on the
Supply-Secretary of State rather farfetched assumption, I think, that the people concerned were making some contribution to the war effort. I know some friends of mine received awards. They certainly deserved them, but if you are going to apply the yardstick of the war effort I would suggest that everyone who was not in jail or a saboteur was probably contributing something to the war effort. If you made awards on that basis you would have a fairly liberal list from which to choose.
This practice was discontinued shortly after the war, and when I took up the matter of this lady whom I mentioned earlier with the Secretary of State I found rather to my surprise that orders of the British Empire of the various ranks were reserved entirely for the military. I have no objection whatsoever to these awards being given to those in the armed services. I think it is perfectly fitting they should receive them.
But I do suggest this. If it is found desirable, and apparently it has been, to confer upon those in the employ of the state these various awards from time to time, then there is all the more reason why they should be conferred upon those who are not in the employ of the state. Certainly in Great Britain, and I believe in Australia and New Zealand, there is a civilian list. I am not sure of the seniority of the titles, but there is the O.B.E., the M.B.E. and C.B.E. I should like, sir, to see that civilian list restored in Canada, so that certain recognition could be given.
I am not overlooking the fact that we have the George Medal which is, I understand, an award given to civilians rendering acts of valour. For instance, if a farmer pulls someone out of a burning aeroplane or somebody rescues a person from drowning, then the George Medal is a fit and proper award and one which we recognize should be given. But it is given only for valour. I am not overlooking the fact that I have heard -I am sure the Secretary of State has much greater knowledge of this than I have-that there is such an order as the Canada Medal. I must say that is a rather forbidding and awesome sounding title, a rather metallic sound. It is reminiscent of the prize a farmer gets for exhibiting a bull at a fair. I believe we could have chosen a better title.
Nevertheless, I understand that at one time, and the Secretary of State is probably conversant with this in another role, we did establish something called the Canada Medal. I have heard from someone who was supposed to be well informed that there was a time when the government of Canada was confronted with a list of those to whom the Canada Medal might have been awarded. The

Supply-Secretary of State ones responsible for the government of Canada said, "enough". The list was never considered and no promulgations were ever made. Even if the lists for the Canada Medal were promulgated, I believe it would serve the purpose I have in mind.
I do not intend to take the time of the committee in making further mention of this matter. I speak of it because we have a new Secretary of State and one whom I know, because of his background, is conversant with the problem of this government in connection with the matters to which I am referring. I believe he, too, might feel that something of this nature could be done. I am urging that the time has come when action should be taken. We had it, then dropped it for various reasons and I am not going into those. There might have been a personal predeliction on one person's part, but I do say the time has come when we should re-establish those things.

Perhaps in view of the fact the hon. member will have to leave us for another engagement I might say just a word, not about the principle of what he said because it is not for me to discuss that at all.
Why?
I am not the adviser of the crown in matters of this kind.
You are the gentleman in charge.

The Prime Minister has heard the hon. gentleman's remarks, and no doubt has taken note of them. There are a couple of things the hon. member said in the course of his remarks to which I thought I should refer so there will not be any misunderstanding.
The hon. gentleman, I know, did not have the slightest intention of misrepresenting the actual situation, but the actual situation is that these awards in the orders of chivalry- not those that carry a title, but those that do not-are not made to the armed forces generally but are made only to people who have served in an actual theatre of hostilities. There have been no such awards made since the period right after the end of the war for service in an actual war theatre, except for service in Korea. I believe the house and the country ought to understand that because I do not believe that it would be defensible at all to suggest that soldiers or airmen or sailors who served in Canada only should receive this distinction when civilians do not. Whatever may be thought about the wisdom


of that distinction, that is the distinction that is made and not the one the hon. member suggested.
In so far as the Canada Medal is concerned, I understand, in fact I recollect rather distinctly that the approval of the sovereign was given to the institution of a Canada medal. I presume it may be said to exist en principe but in fact none of them has ever been awarded. It has never been my responsibility to consider this matter. It is not the responsibility of the Secretary of State to consider it.

I am going to say a few words about an altogether different matter, but perhaps I should say in passing that I hope we will not go any farther in the giving of titles or awards than we have gone already. Personally, I do not believe that they add to the distinction of the individual who receives them. Very few people know that you have the title, anyway, and that takes away some of the value of receiving it. I have no doubt that it would sound well, for instance if the Prime Minister were called Sir Louis St. Laurent. I think, however, the title he has now is one he would like much better and is probably one that becomes him even better, and that is "Uncle Louis".
The Queen did not confer that one.
The people conferred it, and with all due regard to the Queen it is possibly a higher distinction.
By some people, but not all.

Well, the rest did not demur, and I want to be included amongst the rest who did not.
What I am going to speak about, Mr. Chairman, is what I consider a great miscarriage of justice. I refer to the properties which were confiscated-I use that term but perhaps it is not the correct one-from persons of Japanese origin who were removed from the Pacific coast. I discuss it now for several reasons. I wrote several letters to the predecessor of the present Secretary of State without receiving much satisfaction in the matter. Earlier this session, with one of the property owners concerned and his legal representative, I had a talk about the matter with the minister. The proposals for a review of the case were turned down by the Secretary of State. He informed me to that effect, and I told him I did not agree. He was good enough to say that I could speak about it when the estimates of his

department were before the house; that is one reason why I am taking this opportunity.
I am speaking about it for another reason. I am not a university man, but I was at a special convocation of the University of British Columbia about two years ago, and amongst those present was the Prime Minister who received an honorary degree. The gentleman who made the address at that convocation was Sir John Morris. I think he is a judge of the appeal court in the United Kingdom. There were two sentences in his address which I noted at the time, and which have stuck with me since. He said:
Surely there are few more satisfying experiences than to help set right an injustice. Injustice should be righted' wherever, whenever and however it appears.
There are few people in Canada who would deny that there was an injustice done to these people. Not only was there the injustice of uprooting them from their homes and sending them all over the dominion but there was the injustice of a studied attempt to despoil them of their property.
As I said, no matter how long it is since that happened, I agree with Sir John Morris that injustice should be righted wherever, whenever and however it appears. And there is still another reason why I refer to this. When the event of the removal of these people from the Pacific coast took place we were at war with Japan. There is no denying that Japan was a treacherous and ruthless enemy, and that our people who were unfortunate enough to be taken prisoner or to be caught by the Japanese suffered keenly.
However we have made our peace with Japan. We have signed a peace treaty with her. We have made a soft peace with Japan. And I think that having made a soft peace with Japan we should be big enough and generous enough to make a soft peace with those of Japanese origin in this country, who committed no crime, who committed no treachery, and whose only fault was that they happened at a particular time to be in a particular place, and were of a particular racial origin.
That is my reason for taking up the time of the committee in referring to this matter tonight. The case I am going to refer to was probably the largest property involved in the evacuation. I am not taking up this case because it was the largest; there were hundreds of small properties where the lifework of whole families was lost. That is true of the individual about whom I now speak. He was a naturalized Canadian citizen, naturalized as long ago as 1909. The properties concerned were, among other things, two
Supply-Secretary of State fairly extensive timber limits on Vancouver island. Like the other evacuees, he was given 48 hours notice to leave his property, to get ready and to be transported to some other place in Canada, in this instance the city of Toronto, where he finally landed.
He was not allowed to go back, of course, to look after his property. Yet he was held responsible for everything in connection with it. He was fined because he had not burned the slash, that is the debris left after felling of timber. He had to pay taxes on the property while it was going to ruin, with nobody looking after it. And in that case he was no different from the others.
Where was this?

On Vancouver island. The firm was known as the Deep Bay Logging Company, and the chief shareholder and manager of the property was a person named Ekichi Kagetsu. One piece of property was known as block 195 in the Cowichan lake district on Vancouver island, which he claimed had a market value of $247,500. May I say that Mr. Justice Bird was appointed commissioner to set a value on these properties, and to adjudicate upon their value in 1948, six years after the people were removed. This man was then allowed to go back and prepare the records for his property, but he was given only a very short time to do this and most of the records had been lost. While the value he placed upon it was $247,500 it was sold by the custodian for the sum of $93,000.
The other property was another piece of timberland including 11 blocks of land with a certain amount of felled and cold decked timber, and a stand of immature timber, with some mature timber as well. Mr. Kagetsu put a value upon it of $292,039, and the custodian sold it for $40,000.
I mention this because I am going to show later on the value that was put on some other assets, and it will give hon. members an idea whether a proper price was received by the owners for this property in the sale. It was sold by tender in 1943, I believe, and the attempt at final price settlement was not made until 1948.
Mr. Justice Bird in setting the value took into consideration the amount of timber that was supposed to be on the land; but it is interesting to note that 70 per cent more timber has been cut on the Cowichan lake property, block 195, than the commissioner said was there in the first place. And they were still cutting a couple of years ago.

In the other case 100 per cent more timber was taken off the property than the commissioner said was on it, and they were still cutting on that property in 1951. And then again there was the immature timber which, if left in this man's possession, would have increased in value as the years went by. There were buildings on the property used as bunkhouses for the men working in the lumber camp. The buildings consisted of 20 family residences, 10 bunkhouses, a community hall, a new office and eight other buildings. These were camps. They were insured for $10,000. The commissioner put a value of $1,000 on these buildings. He said the reason that he put that value on them was that the buildings-bunkhouses for the lumber workers to sleep in, and the Kagetsu employees were persons of Japanese origin. The commissioner said that they would not be of any value to an occidental buying the property because the bunks would not be long enough for occidental loggers. It seems to me that that is an amazing way of putting a value on property that you are expropriating or that you are confiscating. Perhaps "confiscating" is not the correct word. It should be the value of the property to the owner, not what it would bring at a forced sale; it should be the value to the man who owned it and controlled it.
Then again there were some railways on the timber limit. There were 8J miles of logging railway, if I remember correctly. Anyone who knows anything about building railways in British Columbia, through the terrain there, knows that it costs money. Not all of this line had rails laid on it, but what did not have rails laid on it had been graded so that a truck could drive over it. For this railway the commissioner allowed the sum of $1,000. If I remember correctly, the reason he gave for that was that the person who was buying the railway would not be using it. That again is an unusual way to put a value on something you are taking from someone and selling at a forced sale. Surely the criterion is the value to the man who owned it, the value it was really to him if he were allowed to use it in his own way for making a living.
No allowance was made for the forcible removal from the property. If that was done to any member of this house what would he think? What would you think of that as justice? You may say it was all done legally; that orders in council were passed and so on. Surely, meeting legal requirements is not meeting the ends of justice. I have before me a statement made by a very well known


gentleman in this country who spoke to the Quebec bar association on January 5, 1953. He said this:
Thus when you are studying present administration of justice or new methods of procedure you are helping your country to preserve, not only justice, but all the fundamental liberties that we have fought for, won and defend as essential to our way of life.
I suppose every hon. member would agree with that. Who said it? No less a person than the Prime Minister of Canada. It is said that the Minister of Justice was at the same meeting and also the solicitor general of the province of Quebec. I agree with the words of the Prime Minister. If what he said is true, then it is high time we reviewed the action we took in providing compensation for the property of people who were forcibly removed from the province of British Columbia and, let me say again, people who had committed no crime and who were never accused of any crime. 1 agree that it is a long time ago, but if we are going to take the words of Sir John Morris that I read before:
Surely there are few more satisfying experiences than to help set right an injustice. Injustice should be righted wherever, whenever and however it appears-*
-here is an injustice that, in my opinion, should be righted. In one of the letters I had from the former secretary of state he said that this property, the Kagetsu property, had not been profitable in the years prior to the evacuation; that is, in 1939, 1940, 1941 and 1942. That was true of a great many properties at that time. But lumbering was a very lucrative business in British Columbia from 1942 at least until quite recently. But again I say that that should not be considered in making a just award for this property. I have before me the report of an arbitration award in the matter of the Beauharnois shareholders in respect of property taken over by the government of the province of Quebec. This statement appeared in the Montreal Gazette of March 21, 1953. The arbitrators had this to say:
We think it is pertinent also to refer to the fact that the Beauharnois undertaking was in 1944 emerging from its lean year-
Let us say that the Kagetsu business in 1942 was emerging from the lean years. I continue:
-a process experienced by nearly every industrial undertaking. It takes time to build up a well-trained operating staff, to iron out operational problems and difficulties.
It is only after such things are done that the profits begin to come in and, as I said before, the same principle would apply in

regard to the Kagetsu property. I would urge the Secretary of State, in taking over his new office, to think of the high regard in which the matter of dispensing justice is held in this country. I hope that we do not only give lip service to justice when making speeches before bar associations or at university convocations, but that it is something we believe in every day of the week.
The minister is a new man, new in his office and new in the government, but there are people in Canada and I am sure people in the present government who I am quite satisfied agree that perhaps next to the expulsion of the Acadians this is the darkest stain on the escutcheon of Canada. I say this committee should give its approval to having someone review this entire matter. The review which was made by the commissioner who made the award in the first place is an altogether amazing way to appeal a case. I would like very much to have this case referred to the exchequer court, where such cases should be referred, and have this matter reviewed by the present president of that court. I would be most interested in what he would have to say.
Is the hon. member suggesting that the procedure in this one particular case where the amount covered is $93,000 should be subjected to review, or does he mean all cases?

I would suggest that in all these cases where there has been an injustice there should be a review. I mention this case because I was consulted in connection with it, and first approached by a solicitor in Vancouver, then by Mr. Kagetsu, and I said-
Did this man appeal his case to the court of appeal or a royal commission?

There was only one appeal in this case as far as I understand, though the Secretary of State may correct me if I am wrong. It was reviewed by the commissioner who set the value on the property in the first place, Mr. Justice Bird of the appeal court of British Columbia, and an appeal was later made to him for revision. He heard the case and made a small adjustment amounting to some $2,000 odd. But in my opinion the appeal should have been sent to some justice outside the province of British Columbia, and the proper court to which appeals should be referred is, in my opinion, the Exchequer Court of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I want
wholeheartedly to support the plea addressed to the Secretary of State by the hon. member
Supply-Secretary of State for Vancouver-Kingsway. I thought he dealt very well with the principles involved and supported them with facts. I had quite a lot to do with these Japanese-Canadians because during the war possibly a majority of them were in various villages and camps in my own constituency. As a matter of fact, on one occasion Mr. Austin Taylor, chairman of the commission, asked me to visit various mining camps with an assistant commissioner of the R.C.M.P. to see in what way they could utilize old hotels, disused houses and so on. He said to me: "From my lifelong experience as a member of the R.C.M.P., I would advise you, Herridge, always to sleep in your underwear to avoid catching cold when you stop at a hotel in a small mining community."
These people lived in my constituency during the war in quite large numbers and I had an opportunity of meeting many of them. The longer they stayed in the district the more their good qualities were recognized and many of these people told me of their losses on account of evacuation in the way of homes, furniture, farms, equipment, boats and so on.
I am quite confident that a considerable number of people have been treated unjustly according to Canadian standards and some of the cases are almost tragic and heartbreaking. Many of these people spent the whole of their lives building up small estates which they had to leave and which were disposed of at fire sale prices. I am going to quote briefly from a brief I have here composed by the evacuation losses compensation committee in order to support the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. This brief has this to say:
For example, one claimant who owned timber limits can at this date prove that twice the volume of timber existed than was allowed by the commissioner. Unshakable B.C. government scale records of timber actually removed from his limits from the date of sale to the present, is weighty new evidence, not available in 1948 to the commissioner. The logging of these limits still continues. The under secretary of state has rejected this new evidence on the patently irrelevant grounds that the claimant's management was inefficient, which contention conflicts with the commissioner's findings. Factors such as closer utilization fail entirely to reconcile the wide disparity. Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who is an old friend of mine, for his courtesy in letting me know well in advance that he was going to bring up this matter. It is true that I received Mr. Kagetsu when the hon. member was present and I think I should tell the committee as nearly as I can recollect it what happened at that time.
The position I took was that I was not appointed to my present office to act as a court of appeal from decisions made by my predecessors or by Mr. Justice Bird, and that I would not attempt myself to assess the merits of a case which, I am only too ready to recognize, I am not competent to assess. I said, moreover, that I was not willing to go to my colleagues and ask them if they would permit a review of this one individual case, for I said I would not be a party to such an injustice; merely because Mr. Kagetsu was one of the largest claimants, and merely because he had greater facilities for bringing his claims repeatedly to the attention of the government, I said I would certainly not ask for a review of his case in isolation; all I would do was to go to my colleagues and ask them if they were prepared to have all the cases reviewed, because it seemed to me that the smallest claim had just as much right to justice as the largest one.
I told Mr. Kagetsu, in the hon. member's presence, and I am sure he will confirm this, that I did not think my colleagues would agree to such a review, but I said I would ask for it though I told them quite frankly why I did not think it would be granted.
I said that the most competent person the government of the day felt it could select had been selected from the bench of the province of British Columbia to make a review of all these cases. That person had made an adjudication which I was sure was as objective and as dispassionate as any judge could make.
Whether he made mistakes or whether he did not make mistakes, I do not know. Of course all of us are human and all of us occasionally make mistakes. I do not yield to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway in my passion for justice. But the only way in which justice can be rendered is by human beings who are liable to err. Judge Bird may have made some mistakes but he made as judicial and as dispassionate a consideration of these claims as I think anyone would be apt to make. I am not at all convinced- and neither were my colleagues-that to have them reviewed by another judge or by two or three judges would eliminate any,
[Mr. Herridge.J

if there were any, or all, if there were a number, of the errors that Judge Bird may or may not have made. It seemed to me that it was just a question of whether the government had reasonable confidence that Judge Bird had done as good a job as could reasonably be expected to be done in all the circumstances. My colleagues had come to the conclusion, before I became a member of the government, that that was so and they were not prepared to change that view. I must say that in the light of all the circumstances I concur in that view.
May I ask the Secretary of State one question?
Certainly.

Why did the government not apply to these cases the same methods that were applied, for instance, in expropriating one of the Booth properties in Ottawa or the Edwards property or the Perley property? Why did they not apply the same principle, put a value on the property and then if the person concerned was not satisfied with the value he could appeal to the exchequer court? Why was this sort of policy adopted: Here it has to go before the commissioner; you take it or you leave it.
That is a question I would not attempt to answer.
There is no answer to it.

I am no more capable of interpreting the minds of other people than is my hon. friend. I was not a member of the government when this decision was made. It was made by a government of which I was not a member and it is impossible for me to say why the government did one thing rather than another. It did a thing which I know was intended to be fair, which I believe was substantially fair, and which the government is not prepared now, at this late date, to change.

The discussion of the estimates of the Secretary of State has got off on this subject of the awards made to the Japanese who were dispossessed of their property by order in council passed during the war, under which a judge of the appeal court of British Columbia was appointed to adjudicate as a commissioner. I think probably no more interesting and no more appropriate subject could have been chosen for the institution of the discussion of the estimates of the new Secretary of State of Canada.
At the outset I want to say that I feel that the action taken by the government of Canada with respect to the suspected disloyal activities of the Japanese on the Pacific coast was,

by and large, a proper and a fair action to take. As I understand it-I was not here at the time-it had the support of the majority of the citizens on the coast at that time. Therefore in so far as the Japanese being removed from their properties on the coast and sent to other areas of the country where they could not do any damage to the war effort is concerned, I have no criticism to offer of the government of the day.
But having said that I think it is essential that we should realize that now that the war is finished, now that we are in conflict with another ideology, namely that of communist Russia, we should be, so far as it is possible, above and beyond reproach. That is a difficult thing, but in so far as we can do it I think we should say to ourselves that where these men were dispossessed of valuable property to which they were at that time lawfully entitled we as a Christian and democratic state will restore them to the position in which they would have been had this unfortunate measure not been necessary. I doubt very much if there are many in this house or in the country who would disagree with me in that general statement of objectives. It therefore becomes necessary to review the measures taken to deal with this whole problem.
Tied up with this thing I think is the question of the claims of our own people for maltreatment suffered in the course of the war in the Far East. As it happens, this is also a matter under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State. Here I find that Canadian citizens were subjected to the most unsatisfactory conditions of delay and hardship in respect of the recognition of their claims for war damage on that account. Our complaint against this government is twofold. First, our complaint is that the Japanese who are now Canadian citizens have not been given proper recognition of their just claims for their dispossession. In the second place-and I am even more concerned on this account-Canadian citizens who suffered damage and hardship, loss of physical health-in many cases men or women have claims on account of the death of their husbands or wives, on account of the death of the other party-as the result of Japanese internment in the Far East have not had their claims treated in accordance with their just deserts. On both these counts the Department of the Secretary of State stands indicted.
I have had some considerable lengthy correspondence with the predecessor of the Secretary of State and with the war claims commission operating under the aegis of his department and I have this to say. So far as I am aware, not one single case that I have
Supply-Secretary of State taken up with the war claims commission has yet been settled. Although the war against the Japanese has been over now for nine years, not one single case of a claim for internment, death, loss of property or whatever may be the ground, has yet been settled. Although I fully support the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway in his contention that the Japanese who were dispossessed have not had full justice done to them with respect to the value of their property-I say that in all solemnity; I fully support him in what he has said-I think it is even more reprehensible that Canadians or the wives and widows of Canadians have not had full justice done to them under our war claims commission on the claims that they have with respect to death or internment or loss of property as a result of the war in the Far East.
Having said that, may I say that I hope the Secretary of State will not only take the matter under consideration-I hope he will do that-but will insist on some action. I know he is an energetic, young and vigorous man. Perhaps in that respect he is a little bit different from his predecessor who found it rather hard to stay awake in the House of Commons here.

I do believe it is a position that denies the position taken by most democratic governments, and certainly it is a denial of the position taken by the government of which the hon. gentleman is now privileged to be a member. This government has never hesitated, under the well-known constitutional precedent, to accept responsibility for the decisions which were made by its predecessor, whether or not there happened to have been in the meantime a change of government.
